events.text: Four times a year now, the year hands itself over through you. Eighteen days before each season the old one comes to the middle and sets down what it carried, and the new one picks it up, and for those eighteen days the whole land rests its weight on you. The first hand-over of your new life is summer giving way to autumn.

choices.text: Hold still and let summer set it down

effects.log: Summer comes to the middle hot and tired and full of thunder, and puts it all down on your back: the heat, the long days, the green. You hold it eighteen days. Autumn picks it up gently, as if afraid to wake you. Down below, nobody digs, and the rice dries on the yards without a drop of rain.

choices.text: Ask summer what it is leaving behind

effects.log: Summer, it turns out, is leaving a great deal behind: a drowned field it is sorry for, a boy who learned to swim, a fever that went round the river villages. You listen to all of it. Autumn listens too. The hand-over takes the full eighteen days and is the most orderly in a century.

choices.text: Sleep through it, the way earth does

effects.log: You sleep, and the year goes over you like a cart over a bridge. It does not stumble. You wake in the first frost knowing you were needed only to be there, which is the hardest work you have.

events.text: Spring will not end. It has come to the middle for the hand-over and will not set anything down: one more week of blossom, it says, one more rain, the young barley is not ready. Summer waits at the edge, sweating. In the valleys below the farmers are looking at the sky and frowning.

choices.text: Let spring stay one week more, and no longer

effects.log: One week. Spring spends it like a child at a fair, everything at once: blossom, rain, birdsong, a late frost it immediately regrets. Then it sets the whole armful down on your back and runs. Summer picks it up, grumbling, and the barley is ready after all.

choices.text: Take it from spring yourself and hand it on

effects.log: You do not argue. You simply lift the season out of spring's arms, the way a grandmother lifts a sleeping child off someone tired, and hand it to summer. Spring stands there empty-handed and, after a moment, relieved.

choices.text: Say nothing, and wait

effects.log: You say nothing. Spring talks for three days about the barley. Then, hearing itself, it stops, and sets the season down, and goes. Most quarrels at the centre end this way, you are learning: if you wait, they hear themselves.

events.text: Autumn has come too early. It is at the middle before summer has finished, impatient, with the frost already in its sleeves, and the late rice in the south is still green in the ear. If autumn takes the year now, half a province will go hungry.

choices.text: Hold the hand-over shut for nine more days

effects.log: You hold the gap shut. Autumn pushes. It is like holding a door against a crowd, for nine days, and your whole long body aches with it. In the south the late rice ripens in a rush of warm nights. On the tenth day you let go, and autumn tumbles through, embarrassed. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let autumn in, but warm the south from below

effects.log: You let autumn have the year and send your own warmth up under the southern paddies, the way you once warmed a rice jar. The frost comes down on the north and stops at the edge of the warm ground. The late rice ripens with frost all round it, like an island.

choices.text: Ask autumn why it is in such a hurry

effects.log: "The orchards," autumn says. "The persimmons in the west. The tiger asked." You think about the rice and the persimmons for a day, and send autumn back to wait four days, not nine. Everyone gets most of what they wanted. This is, you suspect, the whole job.

events.text: Winter will not leave. It is the third month and it is still sitting in the middle of the year like an old guest by the fire, very slow, very cold, telling the same story again. Spring is at the door with its arms full. Nobody below has planted anything.

choices.text: Talk winter out of the door, politely

effects.log: You agree with everything winter says. Yes, the snow was beautiful. Yes, the ice on the river was very fine. Yes, it must be tired after such a season. Winter, agreed with for a whole week, finds it is tired, and goes to bed in the north, and spring comes in all at once.

choices.text: Grow warm under it until it has to move

effects.log: You warm the ground under winter the way a hearth warms a floor, slowly and without argument. Winter shifts, and shifts again, and at last gets up muttering that the middle of the year has gone soft. The thaw comes in a single night.

choices.text: Let winter finish its story

effects.log: You let it finish. It takes nine days. The story is about a frozen river and a child who crossed it and should not have, and it is very sad, and at the end winter gets up and goes, lighter. The planting is late, but it is not lost. (-4 health)

events.text: In a valley below, an old farmer keeps the eighteen days for you. No spade goes into the ground, no wall goes up, no grave is moved. Every day of the eighteen the old farmer comes out at dusk and pours a little water on the middle of the yard, and says, to nobody, that it is a long job and somebody has to do it.

choices.text: Warm the yard under the old farmer's feet

effects.log: The yard goes warm under the old farmer's bare feet. The old farmer stands very still, then laughs out loud, alone in the dusk, and goes in and tells nobody, and pours the water out a little more carefully the next day.

choices.text: Send the farm a year that knows what it is doing

effects.log: The rain comes when it is wanted and stops when it is not. The harvest is not large, but it is exactly enough, and dry, and in on time. The old farmer says to the neighbours that it was a year that knew what it was doing. You take that as the best review you have ever had.

events.text: Once, only once, the year hands itself over without you. You are elsewhere, at the edge of heaven on some business of the centre, and in the eighteen days before winter the old season comes to the middle and finds it empty. When you come back, winter has already arrived.

choices.text: Ask how it went

effects.log: It went badly, and then well. Autumn waited in the empty middle for nine days, not knowing what to do, and then winter came and took the year out of its arms anyway, a little roughly. There was an early frost. Nothing died that could not be replanted. You understand, with a pang, that the year can do this without you. That is good. It is also very strange.

choices.text: Promise yourself you will not leave the middle again

effects.log: You promise. It is a heavy promise, and you feel it settle on your back with everything else. The next hand-over goes perfectly, with you in the middle, holding it. You are not sure whether that was the lesson.

choices.text: Leave the middle empty again next year, on purpose

effects.log: You stay away on purpose, the next year, and watch from the edge. Autumn waits in the empty middle, less frightened this time, and hands the year to winter almost gracefully. The frost comes on time. You come back lighter than you left.

events.text: The wheel is grinding. You can feel it in every hand-over now: one phase too strong, one too weak, the seasons coming to the middle lopsided, like porters with a load on one shoulder. This year it begins. The wells in the eastern counties go dry one by one, and the rice stands brown in cracked paddies, and the farmers look at the ground, at you, and do not understand.

choices.text: Turn the wheel, hard, while you still can

effects.log: You lean on the wheel like an ox on a millstone. It moves a little. In the east a spring comes back in one village, then another. It is not enough. The wheel grinds back toward where it was, and you feel the next calamity coming the way old earth feels rain.

choices.text: Lie still and listen to where it is uneven

effects.log: You listen. Wood, fire, earth, metal, water: one is shouting, one is barely breathing, the others are quarrelling over the gap. It is like a family with one child grown too big and one forgotten. Knowing it does not fix it. But you know now what is coming.

events.text: Next, a cold, wet summer. The hearths in the north will not stay lit, the rain never stops, the rice never ripens. Water has quenched fire. The almanac-makers at court are burning their own almanacs to keep warm, which the court chroniclers say is a joke and is not.

choices.text: Warm the ground under the northern villages

effects.log: You spend yourself warming the ground under forty villages, a hearth at a time. The rice still fails. But nobody freezes, and in spring the seed rice in the lofts has not rotted, because the floors were warm. It is something. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let it run its course, and save your strength

effects.log: You let the cold summer run. It is the hardest thing you have done since you were clay. You hold your strength for what comes next, and you feel every cold hearth above you like a stone in your side.

events.text: Then fire melts metal. A summer of fires, and the great armoury of the capital burns with half the kingdom's spears and plough-blades in it. The smiths stand in the ashes holding lumps of melted iron, and somebody in the crowd says aloud that the old dragon of the centre has stopped caring.

choices.text: Rise in the smoke, once, so they see you care

effects.log: You rise out of the ashes of the armoury in the smoke, gold and enormous, for the space of a breath, and sink again. Ten thousand people see it. Nobody says you have stopped caring after that. The smiths go back to work with a strange stubborn hope.

choices.text: Cool the ground under the forges, quietly

effects.log: You draw the heat down out of the forges and into yourself, all through the summer. The new plough-blades come out tempered and true. Nobody knows why. You burn a little, inside, for years.

events.text: Then metal cuts wood. The armies go out, as they always do after a bad harvest, through the forests and over the hills, and the hills are stripped for charcoal for the forges, and the slopes come down in the rain. You lie under it all and count the trees, the way a mother counts children.

choices.text: Hold the bare slopes together with your own back

effects.log: You put your back under the bare slopes and hold them while the rains come, one valley after another. Most of them stay up. The ones that come down come down slowly, and the villages under them have time to run. You are bruised all along your length. (-8 health)

choices.text: Draw the armies away with an omen

effects.log: A yellow light over the generals' tents, three nights running. The soothsayers are terrified, and the armies go home without a battle, and the forests stop falling. It costs you nothing but your good name with the soothsayers, who now say yellow light means retreat.

events.text: Last, wood breaks earth. The roots split the terraces, and in the summer rains the fields slide downhill, and this time you feel it in yourself. A crack, deep down, running through the middle of you like a crack through a jar. The centre is splitting.

choices.text: Hold the crack shut with everything you have

effects.log: You hold it. It does not close. But it does not widen, either, while you hold it. Above you the fields go on sliding. You understand that you cannot hold the crack and the fields at the same time, and that soon you will have to choose. (-10 health)

choices.text: Feel where the crack goes

effects.log: It goes five ways. Of course it does. A blue seam toward the east, a red toward the south, white toward the west, black toward the north, and the yellow, which is you, staying in the middle with nothing to hold it together. If it opens, you will not die. You will become five.

events.text: The crack runs five ways through you, and the wheel is grinding itself apart over your head. You could still hold. You could set down everything else and give your whole strength to the middle. Or you could let go, and come apart into five lesser dragons of the five colours, and each of you go to one end of the land and make its weather, and nobody would hold the middle any more.

choices.text: Set everything else down and hold the middle

effects.log: You give away every other burden you carry, all at once, to whoever is nearest: ministers, elders, an astonished heir. Then you put your whole strength into the middle and hold. The crack stops. It does not heal; it stops. The wheel grinds on, unevenly, but it turns. You have time now, a little. The houses above sag where you let go of them. (-12 health)

choices.text: Ask the five phases, one by one, to forgive each other

effects.log: It is an absurd thing to do, and you do it: you speak to wood about earth, to earth about water, to fire about metal, like a grandmother with five sulking grandchildren. Nothing forgives anything. But the grinding slows, and slows, and for one whole year the land below has ordinary weather.

choices.text: Let go, and come apart into five

effects.log: You let go. The crack opens with no sound at all, and you are five: a blue dragon flying east to make spring rain, a red one south to make the summer, a white one west for the autumn frost, a black one north for the snow, and a small yellow one that wanders in the dust and does not know where to stop. The weather goes on. Nobody holds the middle any more.

events.text: News comes down the roads the way cold comes down a valley: horsemen from the steppe have crossed the northern river. They burn every temple from the border, one after another, and the smoke goes up like a row of beacons coming south. Over your heart the nine-storey pagoda stands as it has for centuries.

choices.text: Lie very still under the pagoda and listen to the roads

effects.log: You listen. Hooves, far off, more than you can count; carts of plunder; and under it, very thin, the chanting of monks who have not run yet. The pagoda over you creaks in the wind. You have held it up through lightning twice. You do not know how to hold it up through fire.

choices.text: Send a tremor up the pagoda, a warning

effects.log: The nine storeys shiver, top to bottom, and every bell on every eave rings at once in a dead calm. The monks come running out into the courtyard. The abbot looks at the pagoda, then at the ground, and understands, and sends a novice running for the scripture boxes.

events.text: The abbot comes down into the crypt under the centre pillar at night, alone, with one lamp, and kneels on the stone over you. "They built the nine storeys so that nine enemies would never come," the abbot says. "The enemies are coming. Was it a promise? Or only a hope? I need to know before I tell the monks to stay or go."

choices.text: Say: it was a hope. Go

effects.log: "It was a hope," you say, from under the floor. "Hopes do not hold back horses. Go." The abbot weeps, once, and then gets up and is an abbot again, and by morning the monks are packing the scriptures into ox-carts. Nobody will die for a pagoda in this temple if you can help it.

choices.text: Say: the promise was mine, not the wood's

effects.log: "The promise was mine," you say. "Not the wood's. The wood may burn. I will still be here." The abbot is silent a long time. Then: "Then the monks may go, and you will stay." Yes. You will stay. You feel the weight of it settle on you like snow on a roof.

events.text: The horsemen are two days away. The monks have the scriptures in ox-carts, three hundred boxes of them, and the only road south crosses the open plain, where the horsemen's scouts ride. The carts will be seen from a day off.

choices.text: Raise a fog off the river for two days

effects.log: You breathe up a fog off the river and the paddies, thick and yellow-white, and keep it lying on the plain for two days and two nights. The ox-carts creep south through it at walking pace. The scouts ride within a bowshot of them and see nothing. On the third morning the fog lifts, and the plain is empty.

choices.text: Shake the road behind the carts so the horses will not take it

effects.log: You shiver the ground under the southern road the moment the last cart is past, and the horsemen's ponies, who know the earth better than their riders, refuse it, rearing and screaming. The riders take the long way round. The scriptures get away. The horsemen remember the road that would not be ridden.

choices.text: Let the monks choose their own road

effects.log: You do nothing, and the monks choose the mountain road, which you would not have chosen, which is narrow and slow and which the horsemen never think to ride. They get away. You are humbled. The people on top of you sometimes know things you do not.

events.text: The horsemen are at the temple gate. Their general rides in alone first, a hard old soldier with frost in the beard, and looks up at the nine storeys for a long time. Then down, at the ground, as if he too can feel something under it. Behind him his officers are lighting torches.

choices.text: Rise into the courtyard and face the general

effects.log: You come up out of the courtyard flagstones, gold and enormous, and the general's horse throws him. He lies on the stones looking up at you, and does not reach for his sword. "I know what you are," he says, in a language you nonetheless understand. "It changes nothing. I have orders." But his torches go out in his officers' hands, all of them, and it takes them until dusk to light new ones.

choices.text: Stay under the stones, and let the general look

effects.log: The general looks. He gets off his horse, and walks once round the pagoda, and puts his hand on the centre stone, and takes it away quickly, as if it were warm, which it is. "A pity," he says to nobody. Then he goes back out to his officers, and you hear the torches being lit.

events.text: The pagoda burns. It goes up storey by storey like a lamp being lit from the bottom, nine floors of centuries-old pine, and the bells on the eaves ring as they fall. You lie under it with the heat coming down through the stones and feel every beam. The golden hall goes too, and the gold on its beams runs down the steps like honey.

choices.text: Hold the centre pillar up until the last moment

effects.log: You hold it. You hold the burning pillar up through the floor of the world while the nine storeys burn round it, so that the last monks hiding in the bell pavilion have time to run. Near dawn the pillar comes down. It falls straight, into the socket, the way it went up. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let it fall, and save your strength for the ground

effects.log: You let it burn. You put your strength instead into the ground under the town, so that the fire does not go through the roots of the houses. The pagoda falls. The town, mostly, does not. You will never be sure that was the right choice. (-6 health)

events.text: The horsemen have ridden on. Where the nine storeys stood there are sixty-four stones in the ash, and in the middle the great centre stone, its socket full of rainwater from the first storm after the fire. The temple will never be rebuilt; you know it the way you know the seasons. You could go on. Or you could stay here, under the stones, for ever.

choices.text: Go on, to the next thing that needs a centre

effects.log: You rise out of the ash at last, slowly, and turn your face to the rest of the land. Behind you the rain fills the socket of the centre stone. You will come back to look, sometimes. It is not a grave. It is a place where something stood.

choices.text: Stay a hundred years, then go on

effects.log: You stay a hundred years under the stones, mourning in the way earth mourns, which is by growing grass. When you rise again the sixty-four stones are deep in green and children are jumping on them. That is enough. You go on.

choices.text: Stay under the sixty-four stones for ever

effects.log: You stay. You held it up through lightning and tilt and all the centuries, and when the horsemen burned it you stayed, and you are staying now. You lie under the sixty-four stones in the grass, and the socket of the centre pillar is always full of rainwater, even in drought, even in winter, and sometimes a child sits on the centre stone and feels it breathe.

events.text: The great bell of the burned temple survived the fire: four times the size of any other bell in the kingdom, lying cracked-free in the ash. The horsemen's general wanted it left. He was overruled. Now three hundred soldiers are rolling it east on logs, toward the sea, to ship it home as plunder.

choices.text: Make the bell heavy

effects.log: You lean into the bell from below, and it grows heavy, then heavier. The logs crack under it. Three hundred soldiers become six hundred. The general, riding behind, watches with an expression you cannot read, and once, quietly, smiles.

choices.text: Go with it under the road, mile by mile

effects.log: You follow it under the road, a mile a day, the way a dog follows a cart that has its master's coat in it. You do not know yet what you will do. You know only that you will not let it go to the sea alone.

events.text: The lowest pass over the eastern ridge. The soldiers are hauling the bell up the last slope on ropes, cursing, and below on the other side you can see the river running down to its mouth on the eastern sea, and a ship waiting there with its sails furled.

choices.text: Soften the slope so the bell rolls back

effects.log: The road under the bell goes soft as porridge. It rolls back down the slope, scattering soldiers, and it takes them nine days to haul it up again. You have bought nine days. You are not sure what for.

choices.text: Let them haul it over, and save your strength

effects.log: You let it go over the pass. It rings once at the top, by itself, a long low note that the whole eastern coast hears, and the soldiers stop hauling to listen, and some of them take off their helmets. Then they haul it down toward the sea.

events.text: The river mouth. The soldiers have built a ramp of logs out to the ship, and they are rolling the bell up it in a cold wind. The ship sits very low in the water. The tide is turning. The old fishermen of the river mouth are watching from their boats, and none of them thinks the ship will float.

choices.text: Hold the ramp steady so nobody is crushed

effects.log: You hold the ramp under the bell steady while three hundred men push, and not one of them is crushed, though the logs groan like animals. The bell goes aboard. The ship settles lower, and lower. The general, on the shore, takes off his helmet.

choices.text: Ask the sea to take it gently, if it must

effects.log: You speak to the sea, which is not yours, the way one old thing speaks to another. The sea does not answer. But the wind drops, and the waves at the river mouth go long and smooth, as if listening, and the fishermen in their boats look at each other.

events.text: A mile out, the ship founders. It goes down slowly, the bell taking it, and the soldiers are in the water swimming for the boats, and the fishermen are pulling them in, enemies or not. The bell is sinking into the deep water at the river mouth. You could let it go. Or you could go down with it, and keep it company, and ring it.

choices.text: Bring the drowning soldiers in to shore

effects.log: You rise under the swimmers like a sandbank and carry them in, every one, to the shingle. The general counts his men on the beach and finds them all there, and looks out at the water where the bell went down, and bows to it, and rides away north without a word.

choices.text: Let the bell go, and remember its note

effects.log: You let it go. It goes down into the dark, ringing once, very faintly, as it touches the bottom. You keep the note. In the years after, when you need to remember something exactly, you hum it to yourself, and it works.

choices.text: Go down into the sea with the bell

effects.log: You go down with it. You leave the land and go down into the cold water at the river mouth and coil round the great bell in the dark, so that it will not be alone. On stormy nights, when the fishing boats are caught outside the harbour, you ring it, slow and steady, and the fishermen hear it under the waves and steer for the sound, and come home.

events.text: You come back, after a long time, to the place where the nine storeys stood. Sixty-four stones in the long grass, and in the middle the centre stone with its socket full of rainwater. It has not rained for a month. The water is there anyway. You know why: you never quite left.

choices.text: Lie under the stones a while, the way you used to

effects.log: You lie under them. It fits, the way an old coat fits. The grass grows over your back. The rainwater in the socket shivers once, as if remembering something, and is still.

choices.text: Warm the stones and go

effects.log: You warm the sixty-four stones from below until they are pleasant to sit on, the way a stove is pleasant at the end of a day, and go. Behind you, a farmer who has been resting there all afternoon sits down on the centre stone without knowing why, and sighs.

events.text: Children have found the ruin. They play a game on the stones: jump from one to the next without touching the grass, all sixty-four, and whoever gets to the centre stone first is king. A small one, the slowest, keeps falling off at the forty-third.

choices.text: Lift the forty-third stone a finger's width for the small one

effects.log: The next time the small one jumps, the forty-third stone is a finger's width nearer. The small one lands, and wobbles, and makes it, and makes the forty-fourth, and runs the rest, and stands on the centre stone shrieking with joy. You feel it in every stone. You have not been so happy in a century.

choices.text: Let the game be the game

effects.log: You leave the stones where they are. The small one falls off at the forty-third all summer, and gets up, and tries again, and at the end of the summer makes it, alone, at dusk, with nobody watching but you. That is better. You knew it would be.

events.text: An old farmer brings a cow to graze among the sixty-four stones every afternoon, and sits on the centre stone to smoke a pipe. Today the farmer knocks the pipe out on the stone, leans down close to the socket full of rainwater, and says: "I know you are there. My grandmother knew. I just wanted to say: the grass is good this year."

choices.text: Answer with a warm breath through the stone

effects.log: The centre stone goes warm under the old farmer, all at once, like a hand on a back. The farmer laughs, a dry old laugh, and pats the stone twice, and says, "Good, good," and goes on smoking. The cow does not look up. Cows know.

choices.text: Let the grass answer

effects.log: You say nothing, and the next spring the grass among the sixty-four stones is the best in the province, thick and sweet, with clover in it. The old farmer's cow gets fat. The old farmer gets the point.

events.text: There is a terrace of cloud at the top of the world, among the stars, and you have come up to it the way earth comes up in a spring: slowly, from below. Four seats stand at its four sides. The middle is empty. The first guardian to come is the east, in a blue storm, the Azure Dragon's banner snapping in its own wind. It looks at the empty middle, and at you, and waits.
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Lie down at the edge of the terrace, not the middle

effects.log: You lie down at the edge, by the stair, the way a new servant stands by the door. The blue storm watches you a long time, and then, to your surprise, rumbles something that might be approval. The middle stays empty. It is not yours yet. It may never be.

choices.text: Bow to the east

effects.log: You bow to the blue banner. The storm, which has been in a great many councils, is not used to being bowed to by newcomers, and rains a little in embarrassment. You will learn that the east is like that: very grand, and easily touched.

choices.text: Shut your eyes and listen, with the patience of farmland

effects.log: You shut your eyes. The storm rumbles on at the edge. Under the cloud, very far down, you can feel the whole land breathing, the fields and roads and the five-day markets and the farmhouses with their warm jars. You listen to all of it. It is going to be a long council.

events.text: The second to come is the west, in a white frost: the White Tiger's banner, stiff with rime, a long docket of cases rolled under it. The frost goes once round the terrace, very slowly, and stops in front of the empty middle, and looks at it the way a tiger looks at a gap in a fence.
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Say nothing at all

effects.log: You say nothing. The frost waits. You go on saying nothing. At last it goes to its own seat in the west and sits down with a sound like ice settling on a pond, and you feel, quite clearly, that you have passed something.

choices.text: Ask the west what is in its docket

effects.log: "Ghosts," says the west. "Mostly ghosts. And whether I was ever just." It does not say more. It goes to its seat and unrolls the docket, a little, as if to show you the length of it. It is very long.

events.text: The third is the south, the Vermilion Bird's banner, red as a hearth, and it is singing. It sings its way round the terrace and sets fire to the minutes of the council's clerk in passing, by accident, or not, and sits down in the south still singing, and the song, you realise, is its record: everything it has done, set to music.
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Listen to the whole song

effects.log: It takes a day and a night. It is very beautiful and not entirely accurate. At the end the south looks at you, waiting for applause or a verdict, and you give it neither, only a long breath like wind over barley. The south seems to find this more flattering than either.

choices.text: Put out the burning minutes with a little rain

effects.log: A small rain, over the clerk's desk only. The minutes stop smouldering. The south laughs, delighted, and does not do it again for a whole week, which the clerk says is a record.

events.text: The last is the north: the Black Tortoise's banner, black as a winter night, coming up the stair so slowly that the other three have time to quarrel twice before it arrives. Beside it a long brush rests on the cloud, and there is a dry voice and a slow voice arguing about how to write down the date.
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Wait for the north as long as it takes

effects.log: You wait. The north takes most of a season. When it is seated at last, the slow voice says, to the terrace in general, that it has never been waited for so patiently, and the dry voice says that it has never been waited for at all, and both of them write it down.

choices.text: Ask the north to read you the date

effects.log: The slow voice reads the date. The dry voice corrects it. They are both right, from different calendars. You find this very restful. You suspect the north is the one of the four you will understand best.

events.text: The grey clerk of the council, brush behind one ear, whose minutes the south set alight, explains how it works, since nobody else will. "They bring their cases to the middle," the clerk says. "Rain, frost, songs, slow winters. Whoever holds the middle hears them, one at a time, and gives a verdict. For a long time nobody held it. They brought the cases to the empty middle anyway, and shouted at it."
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Ask what the empty middle answered

effects.log: "Nothing," says the clerk. "Which is why they kept coming back. You cannot win an argument with nothing." The clerk looks at you sidelong. "You could try being a little more than nothing," the clerk says. "Not much more."

choices.text: Ask who held it before

effects.log: "Nobody, in my time," says the clerk. "Once, for a season, a human stood there. It was very brave and very silly and it helped." The clerk writes something in the minutes. "The four have been quarrelling about you since you came up the stair. It is the nicest quarrel they have had in an age."

events.text: The four are seated at the four sides. The middle is still empty, and they have stopped quarrelling, all four, and are looking at it, and at you lying by the stair. Nobody says anything. It is not a test. It is the way a family looks at the empty place at the table when the last one comes in from the fields.
events.arc: The Four Come to the Centre

choices.text: Shut your eyes and pretend to sleep

effects.log: You shut your eyes. You are not asleep. The four know you are not asleep. After a while the east starts talking about the spring rain again, and the west answers, and the south hums, and the north writes it down, and the middle is still empty, and somehow it is a council now, because you are there pretending not to be.

choices.text: Move one length nearer the middle

effects.log: One length. The cloud under you is warmer. All four banners stir together, the way grass stirs together in a wind, and settle again. Nobody says a word. Next century, perhaps, another length.

choices.text: Say: bring me your cases, one at a time

effects.log: "One at a time," you say, from the edge. "Slowly." There is a long silence, and then the east laughs, a rumble of thunder, and the north says "Good," very slowly, and the clerk sharpens a brush. The cases will begin to come to you now. They are very heavy.

events.text: The east brings its case first, because the east always goes first. It wants a spring that pleases everyone: rain for the rice of the south, dry roads for the west's merchants, a late thaw for the north's ice-houses, and blossom on time for the poets. It has tried for three thousand years. It wants a verdict on how.

choices.text: Hear the whole case, every grievance

effects.log: You hear it all: the poets, the rice, the merchants, the ice-houses, three thousand years of springs that pleased half the land and enraged the other half. The east is out of breath by the end, and a little ashamed of how much it minds. You let it be ashamed for a while. It is good for storms.

choices.text: Ask the east which spring it remembers best

effects.log: The east goes quiet, then tells you about one spring, long ago, when it rained on a single boy's field so he would not have to carry water to it, and the boy looked up and laughed. It pleased nobody else at all. The east still thinks about it. You file that away.

events.text: The quarrel that follows the east's case is the old one. The south wants a long hot summer for its rice, the west wants an early autumn for its orchards, the east wants a wet spring, and all of them have turned to the middle to decide. In the councils of other ages, the clerk mutters, the middle would decline to have an opinion and pretend to sleep.

choices.text: Decline to have an opinion, and pretend to sleep

effects.log: You shut your eyes and breathe slowly, like a field at night. The quarrel goes on above you, louder, then quieter, and then, with nobody to win it in front of, it stops being a quarrel. The east and the west settle it between themselves by dawn, spring wet in the east and the harvest early in the west. It works. It nearly always works. The clerk writes down that you were asleep.

choices.text: Give them one sentence and go back to sleep

effects.log: "Rain on the boy's field first," you say, "and the rest will follow." Then you shut your eyes. The east understands at once, and the others, slowly, from the east's face. The spring that year is wet where it is needed and dry where it is not, and the poets complain, which is how you know it was fair.

events.text: The east has one more grievance, old and sore: the rain it lost to the west long ago, the drought year when the Tiger's frost came early and the east's rain froze in the clouds and fell as hail on its own rice. It has never been settled. Both banners stiffen when it is named.

choices.text: Ask the west to speak to it, not you

effects.log: You turn to the white banner and wait. A very long silence. Then the frost says, stiffly, that the hail was an accident, and that it has been sorry for six hundred years, and never knew how to say so. The storm rains for an hour, quietly. That is the settlement. The clerk writes down: settled.

choices.text: Divide the old rain: half a spring to each

effects.log: You give half of one spring's rain to the east and half to the west's orchards, as damages, six hundred years late. Neither is satisfied. Both are less unsatisfied than before. Down in the world, one spring is gentle in the east and the apples are good in the west.

events.text: The east waits for your verdict. It has stopped storming. A blue banner on a terrace of cloud, very still for once, waiting for the middle to tell it whether its springs, all three thousand of them, were well made.

choices.text: Say: well made, if you rain on the boy's field first

effects.log: "Well made," you say, "if you remember the boy's field first, and the poets last." The east thinks about it for a season, and then, at the first hand-over of spring, rains on one small field in a far valley before anything else. The east is heard. The banner bows to the middle, very slightly.

choices.text: Say: you cannot please everyone, and should stop trying

effects.log: The east bristles. It goes off in a black temper and storms on three provinces at once. It will come back. It is not satisfied, and it is not heard; but it has heard you, and that is a start.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the east judge itself

effects.log: You say nothing. The east waits, and waits, and then begins, without meaning to, to judge itself out loud, spring by spring. It is far harsher than you would have been. You will have to hear the case again, and be kinder.

events.text: The west unrolls its docket across the terrace: ghosts. Thousands of them, the restless dead of a thousand years of the west's severity, the executed and the unavenged and the ones it judged too quickly, each a pale light on the cloud. "Judge whether I was just," the White Tiger's banner says. "Nobody else will."

choices.text: Read the docket from the first ghost to the last

effects.log: It takes years. You read every case, every pale light, every frost. Some of them were just. Some of them were not. Some of them were just and terrible at once. At the end the ghosts are very quiet, as if, for the first time, someone had read them all the way through. (-5 health)

choices.text: Ask the ghosts themselves to speak

effects.log: You ask them. Most say nothing; they have forgotten how. A few speak, and what they say is not what the docket says, and not always kinder to themselves. The west listens to its own dead for the first time. Its frost goes thin and grey.

events.text: The west expects you to say nothing. In the councils of other ages, the clerk tells you, the middle said nothing to the west, and the west went away each time unsatisfied and unjudged, and came back. The white banner waits for your silence, already braced against it.

choices.text: Say nothing again

effects.log: You say nothing. The west waits for the silence to become a dismissal, and it does not, because you do not look away. It goes on not being a dismissal for a whole season, until the west understands that you are not refusing to judge it. You are refusing to judge it quickly. The frost goes soft at the edges.

choices.text: Say one thing

effects.log: "Some of them were just," you say. One thing. The west goes so still that the frost on its banner cracks. Nobody has ever said even that much to it. The west takes a long time to think about one sentence, and it is the right length of time.

events.text: One ghost in the docket is different: a woman from a mountain village, executed by the west's frost for a murder she did not do, whose case has been reopened nine times and closed nine times. Her light is the faintest of all. The west asks you, very quietly, what it should have done.

choices.text: Say: it should have listened a tenth time

effects.log: "A tenth time," you say. The west reads the case again, then, in front of you, slowly, the tenth time. Halfway through it stops. It has found the thing it missed nine times. The faint light on the cloud steadies, and brightens, and goes out, gently, like a lamp somebody has finished reading by.

choices.text: Ask the mountain village what it remembers

effects.log: You send down to the village. It remembers her: a good weaver, and a sharp tongue, and a neighbour who hated her. That is enough. The west knows the rest. The ghost on the cloud goes quiet, and stays, to see the end of the case, and then goes.

events.text: The west waits for your verdict. Not about the woman from the mountain village; about all of it. A thousand years of frost. Whether its severity was ever just.

choices.text: Say: just, and too fast. Read every case twice

effects.log: "Just," you say, "and too fast. Read every case twice from now on." The west does. The autumns come a little later after that, and the executions far fewer, and the ghosts of the west begin, slowly, to go home. The west is heard. Its banner bows to the middle, stiffly, like an old soldier.

choices.text: Say: never ask me that again

effects.log: The west goes away, white and stiff. It will ask again. Something that has carried a docket of ghosts for a thousand years does not stop asking because the middle is tired of the question.

events.text: The south brings its case as a song. The Vermilion Bird's record is not written; it is sung, every summer of its life, every fire it lit and every hearth it kept and every county it burned by accident, and it wants a verdict on the song. It sings for nine days. The clerk's minutes catch fire twice.

choices.text: Listen to every verse

effects.log: Every verse. There are verses that are very beautiful and not true, and verses that are true and very ugly, sung in the same voice. At the end you have heard it all, and the south knows you have, and is not sure whether to be pleased or afraid.

choices.text: Ask which verse is missing

effects.log: "Missing?" The south stops singing, offended. Then it goes quiet, and the quiet goes on too long, and at last it sings one more verse, low and short: a county in the far south it burned out of temper, and never sang about. The clerk writes it down. It does not catch fire.

events.text: The south wants a verdict on a song. You have never given a verdict on a song. The other three are watching to see what you will do, the north with particular interest, because the north keeps its record on a shell and has long thought singing it was cheating.

choices.text: Hum one verse back to the south, changed

effects.log: You hum the verse about the burned county back to the south, slowly, the way earth would sing it, and change one line: instead of the fire, the people. The south listens to its own song from the middle, and weeps sparks, and does not burn anything for a year.

choices.text: Ask the north to write the song down

effects.log: The north writes it down, very slowly, on the shell. It takes a decade. The south, hearing its song read back as a record, without the tune, is appalled, and then thoughtful. You did not need to say anything at all.

events.text: The south waits for your verdict, its banner glowing like a banked fire. Was the song true?

choices.text: Say: true, now that the missing verse is in it

effects.log: "True," you say, "now that the missing verse is in it. Sing it every summer with that verse in the middle." The south does. Its summers are a little shorter after that, and kinder. The south is heard. Its banner bows to the middle, and laughs while it does it, which is the south all over.

choices.text: Say: a song cannot be judged, only heard

effects.log: The south is delighted, and the north is disgusted, and nobody is heard. The south will be back with the song next century, slightly longer.

events.text: The north has written its case on its shell, as it writes everything, plate by plate, in tiny slow characters. The dry voice says it will take nine years to read. The slow voice says it will take nine years if nobody interrupts. They both look at the south.

choices.text: Begin reading, slowly, and do not hurry

effects.log: You begin. The first plate is about a river that froze too early and the village that crossed it. It takes a month. You do not hurry. The north watches you read with its slow, ancient attention, and you can feel it relax, plate by plate, like a frozen field in a thaw.

choices.text: Ask the north to read it to you

effects.log: The slow voice reads. The dry voice adds what it meant. Between them it will take rather more than nine years. You settle in. You were made for this.

events.text: Nine years into the reading of the north's shell. You have read seven hundred plates. On the seven hundred and first there is a crack, an old one, mended with something dark, and the dry voice says quickly that it is nothing, and the slow voice says nothing at all.

choices.text: Ask about the crack

effects.log: The slow voice tells you, after a long time: a winter it held too long, out of grief, and a whole province that starved under the snow before it let go. The crack is from that. It mended it itself, badly. You listen. A crack mended, you think, is worth two plates that never cracked.

choices.text: Read past it, and come back to it at the end

effects.log: You read past it, and the north notices, and is grateful, and does not trust you less for it. At the end of the nine years you come back to the crack. By then it is ready to be read.

events.text: The last plate of the shell is read. The north waits for your verdict, perfectly still, snow settling on its banner. It has never once in its long life asked to be judged by anyone. It is asking now.

choices.text: Say: a true record, crack and all

effects.log: "A true record," you say. "Crack and all. Keep the crack." The dry voice makes a noise like ice breaking, which is laughter. The slow voice says, "Good." The north is heard. Its banner bows to the middle, so slowly that it is still bowing at the next council.

choices.text: Say: you did not need me to tell you

effects.log: The north thinks about this for a year and decides it did need you to tell it, and that you have not. It begins, patiently, to read you the whole shell again from the first plate.

events.text: The grey clerk brings a human up the stair to testify: {npc}, an immortal now, who long ago, in a human life, stood in the empty middle of this terrace for one season and held it to the last day. {He} looks at you lying where {he} once stood, and laughs, very softly. "So that is what it was," {he} says. "I always wondered what was holding my hand under the cloud."

choices.text: Ask {him} what it weighed

effects.log: "Everything," says {npc}. "And then, on the last day, a little less, because something under me took some of it." {He} looks at you. "Was that you? Before you were here?" You do not know. You think it might have been. You feel, oddly, lighter for being asked.

choices.text: Thank {him} for holding it until you came

effects.log: {npc} bows to you, and then, after a moment, to the middle, and then to the four. "I was only keeping it warm," {he} says. The four banners stir. The clerk writes it all down and underlines it.

events.text: The grey clerk brings a human up the stair to testify: {npc}, who long ago stood in the empty middle of this terrace for half a season and then stepped out and said plainly that it was not {his} to carry. {He} stands at the edge of the cloud, unsure of {his} welcome. "I set it down," {he} says. "I am not ashamed of it. But I wanted to see who picked it up."

choices.text: Tell {him} that setting it down was the lesson

effects.log: "It was the first thing anyone taught me," you say, "before I was born. That it can be set down." {npc} looks at you a long time, and then sits on the cloud by the stair, the way a guest sits who means to stay a while. You were made lighter by someone being honest. It still works.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stand in the middle again, beside you, for one day

effects.log: {npc} stands beside you in the middle for one day. It is much easier with two. At sunset {he} steps out again, and says so, honestly, and the four banners bow to {him}, all of them, which they have never done for a human.

events.text: The council's roll has a name on it, written under the empty middle long ago and underlined twice: the human who asked every day for a season who belonged in the middle. The clerk brings {npc} up the stair. {He} looks at you and says, with great satisfaction: "There. I asked, and asked, and here is the answer."

choices.text: Say: I heard you, from very far down

effects.log: "I heard you," you say. "Every day. From under the clay." {npc} laughs out loud, and the north writes it down, and the clerk turns the roll round so that {npc} can see {his} own name, and under it, in fresh ink, yours.

choices.text: Ask {him} the same question back

effects.log: "Who belongs in the middle?" you ask. {npc} thinks about it, seriously, for a long time. "Whoever asks that question," {he} says at last, "and does not stop." It is the most useful thing anyone tells you in your first century of the council.

events.text: There is a story in the council's minutes about a human who once stood in the empty middle for a season. The clerk reads it to you, since you asked, and then adds that nobody knows what became of that human, or whether they were real, or only a story the four told to make the middle feel less empty.

choices.text: Hope they were real

effects.log: You hope so. You find you very much want someone to have stood here before you, and held it, and been all right afterwards. That night, half asleep, you feel the faint print of a pair of human feet in the cloud under you, long cold. It is enough.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to add a line: the middle is grateful

effects.log: The clerk adds it, in small careful characters: "The middle is grateful." The south reads it over the clerk's shoulder and does not set fire to it, which the clerk says is the highest honour the minutes have ever received.

events.text: All four directions have been heard. The east, the west, the south and the north sit at their four sides of the terrace, and for the first time in an age there is no case before the middle, no grievance, no song, no shell. Only the four, quiet, and the empty middle, and you beside it.

choices.text: Lie still in the quiet

effects.log: You lie still. The quiet is not empty; it is full, the way a granary is full at the end of a good year. Under the cloud the land below goes on, all its seasons handed over in order. You realise that this, the quiet, is what all the hearing was for.

choices.text: Thank the four, one by one

effects.log: East, west, south, north: you thank them each for their cases. The east rains a little. The west's frost glitters. The south hums. The north begins, slowly, to write it down. The clerk puts down the brush and simply listens.

events.text: The light begins to gather. You did not do anything; it comes on its own, from the four sides of the terrace, blue and white and red and black, running across the cloud toward the empty middle like water toward the lowest place in a field. Where it meets, it is gold.

choices.text: Let it gather, and do not move

effects.log: You do not move. The light gathers in the middle, gold and warm, and some of it spills over you where you lie by its edge, and you feel lighter than you have since you were clay. The four are watching you, not the light. They want to see what you will do with it.

choices.text: Ask the clerk whether this has happened before

effects.log: "Never," says the clerk, who has dropped the brush. "Not in the minutes. The middle has always been dark." The clerk picks up the brush, and puts it down again, and decides some things should not be written until they are finished.

events.text: Before you take a step into the light, there is one question you mean to ask the four. Only one. You have been carrying it since you were the luck of a farmhouse. The four see it in you and go still.

choices.text: Ask: would you judge the same again?

effects.log: "Would you judge the same again?" you ask. The east says no, at once, and laughs. The west says yes, and then, after a long time, no. The south sings that it would sing it differently. The north says it will need nine years to answer, and begins. It is the best answer you could have had: all four of them, still learning.

choices.text: Decide not to ask it yet

effects.log: You keep the question. It is not yet time, or you are not yet brave enough; you cannot tell which. The four relax, a little disappointed. The light in the middle waits, patient as you.

events.text: The four bring you, together, the oldest case of all: not theirs, but the middle's. Who holds the middle when the one who holds it is tired? Who shares the weight of the centre? They have no answer. They want yours before you go into the light.

choices.text: Say: you do. Each of you carries a quarter

effects.log: "You do," you say. "A quarter each, when I am tired." The four look at one another, astonished, and then, one by one, agree. You feel the weight of the centre settle, for the first time, on five backs instead of one. It is so much lighter that you almost laugh.

choices.text: Say: the humans below, a little at a time

effects.log: "The humans," you say. "Elders, ministers, honest scales, an heir who listens. A little at a time." The west frowns; the east is delighted. It is not the old way. It may be a better one. The clerk writes it down twice, once in each column.

choices.text: Say: nobody. That is what the middle is

effects.log: "Nobody," you say. "That is what the middle is for." The four bow, accepting it, and you feel the weight come down on you like a roof. It is a true answer. It is also a very heavy one.

events.text: The council begins to meet around the gold in the middle, not around the empty dark. Cases come, and songs, and shells, and the four bring them to the light and wait. You lie at its edge, close enough to touch it, and listen, and say "Good" now and then without opening your eyes.

choices.text: Say "Good" without opening your eyes

effects.log: "Good," you say, eyes shut, when the east finishes. And when the west finishes. And once, very quietly, when the north has said nothing at all for a whole day. The four come to listen for it. The clerk starts writing it down at the bottom of every page.

choices.text: Open both eyes for one case, and keep them open

effects.log: A small case: a single village drowned by a river the east forgot. You open both eyes for it, which nobody on the terrace has seen you do, and keep them open to the end. The east weeps. After that, every guardian on the terrace knows how to tell when a case matters to you.

events.text: The light has gathered. The circle is closed. Four banners at the four sides, the weight of the land shared out on five backs, and the middle gold and warm and waiting, the way a house waits for the last one in from the fields. The clerk lays down the brush. The four do not speak. It is yours, if you take it.

choices.text: Not yet. Lie at the edge another century

effects.log: Not yet. You lie at the edge another century, and the light waits, and the four do not hurry you. Some things should be taken slowly. You will know when.

choices.text: Go down to the world below a while first

effects.log: You go down for a while to the fields, to the warm jars and the five-day markets, to remember what the middle is for. When you come back up the stair the light is still there, a little brighter, as if it had missed you.

choices.text: Take the centre

effects.log: You go into the light. It closes round you like warm earth round a seed, and the four banners bow, all at once, and you take the place where the four agree. From now on every council of the guardians, in every age, in every life, is held around you, and when they quarrel you shut your eyes, and they hear themselves, and stop.

events.text: News from the deep mountains, carried up to the terrace by a wind: in a pool under a waterfall there is a serpent a thousand years old that has never failed a stage, never eaten a bad meal, never been seen by a human it should not have been seen by. A flawless one. The kind that, the old songs say, heaven lets rise.

choices.text: Go down and lie under its pool, unseen

effects.log: You go down into the bedrock under the pool and lie there, very still, the way you once lay under a jar. Above you, in the cold water, something long and patient is coiled, breathing. It does not know you are there. It is very nearly ready.

choices.text: Ask the four what heaven means to do with it

effects.log: "Let it rise," says the east, which was once something like it. "If there is room," says the north, slowly. Nobody says what happens if there is not. The clerk looks at you, and then at the middle, and then away.

events.text: A human hunter has seen it: a long shape climbing the waterfall at dawn, half out of the water, and fallen back. The hunter told nobody but a grandchild, who told a monk, who told an abbot, who wrote it down, and now the rumour is loose in the world, and a serpent seen by humans before it rises may never rise.

choices.text: Let the rumour die in the archives

effects.log: You let the abbot's page curl and fade in a damp archive until nobody can read it. The hunter dies an old man, smiling. The grandchild grows up and forgets. The serpent in the pool never knows how close it came.

choices.text: Warm the pool so nobody can see into it for the mist

effects.log: The pool steams day and night after that, winter and summer, so thick that nobody climbing the gorge can see the water. The hunters call it the Smoking Pool and stay away. The serpent coils in the warm mist and grows.

events.text: It climbs. One dawn the serpent with no flaw goes up the waterfall and does not fall back, and up the gorge, and up the mountain, and into the clouds, climbing toward the terrace. All four banners turn toward the stair. The whole sky is very quiet.

choices.text: Watch it climb, and say nothing

effects.log: You watch. It climbs well: not fast, not proud, one coil at a time, the way old earth grows. You have never seen anything do it better. You find, to your surprise, that you love it already.

choices.text: Send warmth up the stair under it

effects.log: You warm the cloud stair a step ahead of it, all the way up. It feels the warmth and does not know where it comes from, and climbs a little more easily, and, once, looks back down the stair toward the middle, puzzled.

events.text: It stops just below the terrace. There is no room. The four seats are full, and the middle is spoken for, whether or not you have taken it yet, and a dragon rising needs a place to rise into. The serpent hangs in the cloud under the stair, flawless, a thousand years of patience, and waits, and does not complain.

choices.text: Look for room somewhere else in heaven

effects.log: You ask everywhere: the halls of the seasons, the rivers of stars, the Jade court. Every seat is full. The clerk follows you about, saying nothing, which says everything. The serpent waits under the stair.

choices.text: Lie at the top of the stair, close to it

effects.log: You lie at the top of the stair, as close as you can, and you and the serpent look at each other for a whole season. Neither of you says anything. You think, at the end of it, that it knows what you are thinking about, and is not asking.

events.text: Heaven speaks, for the first time in your hearing, not in a voice but in a change of weight. It asks you, the middle, whether you will make room. If you go down into the earth under the serpent's pool and become the bedrock it rises from, it will rise. If you do not, it will wait, flawless, under the stair, perhaps for ever.

choices.text: Ask heaven for another age to find another way

effects.log: Heaven gives it, without comment, the way the earth gives a season. The serpent waits under the stair. You go on looking for room, and the weight of it sits on you every day you do not find it.

choices.text: Lift it up the last step with your own back, and stay

effects.log: You go down the stair and put your back under it and lift. It rises the last step, and the four seats shift to let it stand among them for one day, as a guest, gold and shaking. Then it goes back down to its pool, rested, to wait for an age with room in it. It knows now that there will be one. (-10 health)

choices.text: Make room

effects.log: You make room. You leave the middle to the four, who will keep it warm, and go down, all the way down, into the earth under the serpent's pool, and spread yourself there, and become the bedrock it rises from. It rises. You feel it go, the weight of it pushing off from your back into the sky. Long after, in another life, a flawless serpent will climb out of a pool and find the ground under it warm, and not know why.

events.text: The house on you is coming apart. The king is a child, the regents are at each other's throats, the provinces are in revolt, and the court has not met in a year without a dagger drawn. Late one night the chief minister comes down into the crypt under the throne hall alone, and kneels, and says only: "Help us."

choices.text: Ask what help the minister means

effects.log: The minister does not know. That is the trouble. Grain, armies, an omen, a miracle, anything. You listen to the whole list. Under it, unsaid, is the thing the minister is afraid to ask for. You can feel it coming the way you feel a season coming.

choices.text: Send the minister home to sleep

effects.log: "Sleep," you say from under the floor. The minister, astonished, goes home and sleeps for the first time in a month. The next day the court is a little less mad. It is not enough. The minister comes back.

events.text: The minister comes back with the whole court: ninety ministers in the rain on the palace terrace, kneeling, holding up the crown on a cushion toward the sky. They want you to come up out of the ground in human form and rule. A dragon on the throne, they say, and the provinces would kneel in a month.

choices.text: Listen to all ninety of them

effects.log: Ninety speeches in the rain. Some are cynical, some desperate, some sincere. One old minister at the back says only: "You would be good at it." That is the one that stays with you. It is true. You would.

choices.text: Rise over the palace so they can see you, and say nothing

effects.log: You rise in the storm over the palace roofs, gold and enormous, and look down at ninety faces looking up. You say nothing. Some of them weep. The crown on its cushion is filling with rain.

events.text: You think about it. You would rule well. You know the whole land the way a body knows itself: every road and granary and market scale, every season's hand-over. No king has ever known as much. And the centre, the old people say, cannot be a king. It can only be the ground a king stands on.

choices.text: Imagine the reign, the whole of it

effects.log: You imagine it, honestly, all of it: the provinces at peace in a month, the granaries full in a year, and then, slowly, the court learning to ask you everything, and the humans forgetting how to decide anything, and the weight of the whole kingdom coming down on your back with nothing under it at all. You see it to the end. It ends with the capital sinking.

choices.text: Ask the oldest minister what a king is for

effects.log: "To be blamed," says the oldest minister, "and replaced." You think about that for a long time. A dragon cannot be replaced. A dragon that is blamed sinks.

events.text: The court waits in the rain for your answer. The crown is on its cushion. The child king, who nobody asked, is standing in a doorway at the back with a nurse, watching.

choices.text: Refuse: the centre is the ground a king stands on

effects.log: "I am the ground a king stands on," you say. "Not the king." You turn to the doorway. "That one. Teach that one." The court is silent, then ashamed, then busy. The regents are given a council of elders to answer to. The child grows up taught by ninety frightened ministers, and is a decent king.

choices.text: Refuse, and give the court a council to share it

effects.log: You refuse the crown, and give them something better: you name nine of the ninety, the honest ones, to share the burden of the regency, and you put a little of your own weight on each. They carry it badly, then better. The provinces come back slowly, over ten years, not in a month. That is the right speed.

choices.text: Take the crown

effects.log: You come up out of the ground in human form and take the crown off the cushion and put it on. The provinces kneel in a month, as they said. The granaries fill in a year. And the weight of the whole kingdom comes down on you with nothing under it, every decision, every hunger, every quarrel, and you feel the capital settle, very slightly, into the ground. (Weight +40)

events.text: The foundation stones of the capital crack in a still night, one after another, with a sound like ice on a river. Nobody is hurt. In the morning the court astrologers stand in the palace courtyard looking at the cracks and do not say what everybody is thinking: the ground under the city is too heavy.

choices.text: Feel where the weight is worst

effects.log: You feel along your own length under the city: here the throne hall, here the granaries, here the yamen of the capital, here a thousand quarrels and decisions you never set down. It is everywhere. It is all of it. You have been holding up the whole kingdom by yourself.

choices.text: Lie very still and hope it passes

effects.log: You lie still. It does not pass. Weight does not pass, it only moves, and nothing moves it off you but setting it down. The cracks stay.

events.text: The palace well goes silent. It has sung, the old servants say, since the palace was built: a little hollow music when the bucket goes down. Now the bucket goes down into nothing, and comes up dry, and the queen's women go to the city wells with jars like everyone else.

choices.text: Give something away, now, to anyone

effects.log: You give the first thing you can reach to the first humans who will take it: the granary decisions to the city elders. They take it, frightened. The well does not sing. But the next crack, when it comes, is smaller.

choices.text: Ask the well what it needs

effects.log: The well, like all water, needs the ground to move. You have not moved in an age. You are holding everything so still that nothing can flow through you. It is not the weight, exactly. It is the holding.

events.text: The capital is sinking. A finger's width a year, then a hand's. The gates no longer close. The palace well is dry. The whole kingdom is resting on you, and you have not set anything down in so long that you have forgotten how. You could try now. Or you could hold it all, and go down with it.

choices.text: Set it down, all at once, to anyone who will carry it

effects.log: You let go of everything you can reach: the granaries to the elders, the courts to the ministers, the roads to the provinces, the succession to a startled heir. Half of it is dropped. A granary empties, a road washes out. But the city stops sinking, and the palace well, after a year, sings once. The house above is poorer for it. (-10 health)

choices.text: Lie fallow a decade and let it ease

effects.log: You stop holding. You lie fallow under the capital for years and let the weight come out of you slowly, the way frost comes out of ploughed ground. The city sinks a little more, then stops. The court never knows how close it came.

choices.text: Hold it all, and go down with it

effects.log: You hold it. You could not set anything down, and you do not now. The ground under the capital sinks into you, gently, the way a cart sinks into a soft road, and stops, and stays. The kingdom stands. But nothing in it grows, or moves, or changes, for three hundred years, and the palace well is silent all that time.

events.text: The tyrant on your back has had you sewn into the robe of state in gold thread and carved over the palace gate, so that every condemned man dragged through it passes under you. You feel every one of them, and the needle in the silk. You stayed with this house too long.

choices.text: Count the ones who passed under the gate

effects.log: You count them. You do not stop counting until you have them all. It takes a year. At the end you know exactly what it has cost to stay, and you can never not know it again. (-5 health)

choices.text: Send the tyrant a dream of the gate

effects.log: You send the tyrant a dream: walking through the gate, under the carved dragon, in chains. The tyrant wakes screaming and has the dream-interpreters beaten. Nothing changes. Some houses cannot be warned.

events.text: The provinces rise. Peasants with flails, soldiers who have changed sides, a general with a grudge. The tyrant wears the yellow robe to the walls every day to show the city whose house this is. The rebels have begun to call yellow the colour of murder.

choices.text: Turn the robe heavy on the tyrant's back

effects.log: The robe grows heavy, then heavier, until the tyrant cannot climb the wall stairs in it, and has to be carried. The city sees its ruler carried in a robe too heavy to bear. Something breaks in the court. Something, very slightly, breaks free in you.

choices.text: Lie still, and feel the city turn

effects.log: You lie still. The city turns, street by street, against the house on your back. You feel every street go, the way a field feels the plough. You do not know yet what you will do when it reaches the palace.

events.text: The capital burns. The rebels are in the palace, and the tyrant is in the throne hall in the yellow robe, and the fire is climbing the red pillars. You are sewn into that robe and carved over that gate. You could tear yourself out of the silk now, and leave the house to fall without you. Or you could stay to the end, as you stayed all along.

choices.text: Tear yourself out of the robe and leave the house

effects.log: You tear yourself out. The gold thread comes away from the silk all at once, in a shower of sparks, and the carved dragon over the gate cracks down the middle, and the tyrant stands in a plain yellow robe in a burning hall, and is only a frightened mortal. You go down into the earth with the stain still on you, but out of the fire. (-10 health)

choices.text: Draw the fire down into the ground, away from the city

effects.log: You cannot save the house and you do not try. You draw the fire down through the palace floors into yourself, so that it does not go out into the streets. The palace burns alone. The city stands. You are scorched all along your back for a century. (-8 health)

choices.text: Stay with the robe, to the end

effects.log: You stay. You stayed too long, and you stay now. When the throne hall burns, you burn with the emblem on the tyrant's robe and the dragon over the gate, and the whole land sees the yellow dragon go up in the smoke of a murderer's house. For a thousand years after, yellow is a colour people are afraid of.

events.text: There are men in the palace courtyard at noon, measuring your shadow. Court alchemists, with knotted cords, pacing out the long gold shape you cast across the flagstones when you rise to bless the house. They are very careful. They write everything down. On a cloth beside them lies a block of green jade the size of a fist.

choices.text: Stop casting a shadow at noon

effects.log: You stop rising at noon. You bless the house at dusk and dawn, when shadows are long and vague. The alchemists measure the courtyard for a month and find nothing, and argue among themselves. But they keep the jade.

choices.text: Let them measure, and watch what they do

effects.log: You let them measure. They take your length, your coil, the angle of your head, and carry it all away on paper to a workshop behind the palace kitchens, where the knives are. You feel the paper go, as if they had taken a little of you with it.

events.text: In the workshop behind the palace kitchens, the alchemists are carving the jade. A coiled dragon on the handle of a seal, cut to the measure of your shadow, one scale at a time. With every scale they cut you feel a small cold place open in you, the shape of a scale.

choices.text: Crack the jade from below

effects.log: You send a shiver up through the workshop floor, and the jade splits across the middle with a sound like a bell. The chief alchemist sits looking at the two halves a long time, then sends for another block. They have more jade than you thought.

choices.text: Sink deeper, out of the measure

effects.log: You sink, a hand's depth, then an arm's, until the shape they have measured is not quite your shape any more. The carving goes on. But the cold places it opens in you are fainter. You are a little harder to bind.

events.text: The seal is finished, and the alchemists have come into the throne hall at midnight with it, and red seal paste, and a brazier, to bind you. They have your measure. They are chanting. You can feel the jade pulling at you like a current, cold and green, and every decree of every king after this will be stamped with what it catches.

choices.text: Break the binding, whatever it costs

ok.log: You come up through the floor of the throne hall in the middle of the chant, and the brazier goes over, and the seal paste burns, and the jade dragon cracks along every scale they cut. The alchemists run. The seal is never finished. In the morning the court finds only a heap of green dust on the throne-room floor, warm.

fail.log: You fight the binding, and it nearly has you. The jade pulls a long cold thread out of you before the brazier tips and the chant breaks. You get away into the deep earth, bleeding gold. The seal lies on the floor of the throne hall, half finished, with a little of you in it. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go down into the deep earth where the jade cannot reach

effects.log: You go down, all the way, into the deep warm places under the land, where no measure reaches. The chant pulls at nothing. The alchemists press the seal on the paper and lift it, and the paper is blank. The house above you is a little weaker for your absence. It is a fair price.

choices.text: Let the jade take you

effects.log: You let it take you. The jade pulls you in, scale by scale, cold and green, until you are coiled in the handle of a seal the size of a fist, and the chief alchemist presses it on red paper and you are on the paper too. Every decree of every tyrant after is stamped with you. You cannot refuse a single one.

events.text: In the north, in an old kingdom that buries its kings in stone chambers under great mounds, a tomb painter has come down into the earth to find you. {npc} kneels in the dark with a lamp and speaks to the ground: {he} has painted a king's tomb, the four guardians on the four walls, and the ceiling is still blank in the middle. "What goes in the centre?" {he} asks. "Nobody can tell me."

choices.text: Say: come back when the walls are finished

effects.log: "Finish the walls," you say from the dark. {npc} jumps, nearly drops the lamp, and then, being a painter, simply nods and goes back up the passage to finish the walls.

choices.text: Send a little gold up through the stone to show {him}

effects.log: A faint gold light comes up through the floor of the tomb passage under {npc}'s knees, the colour of late summer. {npc} stares at it a long time, then gets out a brush and a scrap of paper and starts, very fast, to sketch.

events.text: {npc} has finished the walls of the king's tomb. In the lamplight they are wonderful: the azure guardian on the east wall, the white on the west, the red on the south, the black on the north, each alone in its own field of faded cloud. {npc} lies on the scaffold under the blank capstone, looking up, and asks again.

choices.text: Describe yourself to {him}, slowly

effects.log: You describe it: the coil, the gold, the patience. {npc} listens with both eyes shut, the way a painter listens. "Asleep," {he} says at last. "Or nearly. Content. As if it had decided to stay." Yes. That is it exactly.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the king was like

effects.log: {npc} tells you: a hard king, and a fair one, who liked plums and could not sleep. You think about a king who could not sleep, and how long a tomb is dark. You begin to understand what the painter is asking for.

events.text: The paint is mixed: a gold made of ground stone and something {npc} will not name. {He} lies on the scaffold, brush raised under the capstone, and does not begin. "If I paint you," {he} says, "will you be there? Or only paint?"

choices.text: Say: only paint. Paint it well

effects.log: "Only paint," you say. "Paint it well." {npc} paints all night, and it is very good, and it is paint. In the morning {he} climbs down, satisfied and a little sad. That is an honest answer, and a good tomb.

choices.text: Say: that depends

effects.log: "That depends," you say. {npc} laughs, a short frightened laugh, and puts the brush down, and waits. The lamp burns low. Neither of you moves. The capstone, above, is very blank and very close.

events.text: The last night. {npc} is on the scaffold with the gold, the four guardians are on the four walls, the king is asleep in the dark below, and the capstone in the middle of the ceiling is waiting. You could lend the painter a likeness and go. Or you could go into the stone yourself, and coil there above the four, and keep one sleeper in the dark while the gold fades.

choices.text: Lend {him} a likeness, and go back to the world

effects.log: You hold still in the dark while {npc} paints you, all night, coil by coil. At dawn {he} lies back, shaking. It is the best thing {he} will ever paint. You go back up into the world, and the tomb keeps a picture of you, which is a good thing for a tomb to have.

choices.text: Bless the tomb from outside, and leave it to the four

effects.log: You warm the stone of the whole mound from below, gently, once, and leave the centre of the ceiling to {npc}'s own imagining. {He} paints a dragon that looks nothing like you and is perfect. You are glad you did not interfere.

choices.text: Go into the capstone

effects.log: You go into the stone. {npc}'s brush moves, and you move with it, and the coil closes on itself, head to tail, in the middle of the capstone, above the four guardians on the four walls. {npc} climbs down weeping without knowing why. The tomb is sealed. You keep one sleeper in the dark, for a thousand years, while the gold fades.

events.text: The house on you is old now and small, its king humbled by foreign envoys who walk into the palace without bowing, its treaties written by other hands. The king comes down into the crypt and asks you, not for help, but a question: "Is a small country allowed to stand on its own ground?"

choices.text: Say: you are standing on it
