effects.log: "You are standing on it," you say. "On me." The king is silent a long time, and then laughs, a short hard laugh, and goes back up the stair walking differently. You feel the steps on your back, firmer.

choices.text: Ask the king what standing would cost

effects.log: The king knows exactly: everything, probably, in the end. "But a little while of standing," the king says, "is better than a long while of kneeling." You have no answer to that. You are earth. You have never knelt.

events.text: The king builds a round altar in the middle of the capital, three tiers of stone, in days: a thousand workers, torches all night. A round altar is for heaven. Only emperors sacrifice to heaven. The foreign envoys watch from their compounds and say nothing yet.

choices.text: Hold the altar's foundations steady

effects.log: You lie under the round altar while it goes up and hold every stone where it is set. It is built in days and stands as if it had been there a thousand years. The workers say the ground there is warm, and sleep on it.

choices.text: Lie still and watch what the king will do

effects.log: You watch. The king walks round the altar every night, alone, counting the steps. You can feel the steps. There are a great many of them. The king is very frightened, and goes on.

events.text: Before dawn the king is carried through the capital in a gilded chair on the shoulders of fifty men, to the round altar, and sacrifices to heaven and to earth, which is you. Then the king puts on the yellow. Not the red of a king: the yellow of the centre, a robe embroidered with dragons in gold.

choices.text: Accept the sacrifice to earth

effects.log: You accept it. The offering on the earth tier of the altar sinks into the stone, which no one has ever seen happen, and the ministers gasp, and the king, in yellow, does not flinch. You have accepted the king. You feel the house on you grow heavier, and proud.

choices.text: Let the offering lie, untouched

effects.log: You let it lie. The king looks at the untouched offering a long moment, then puts on the yellow anyway. You think that is the bravest thing you have seen a king do.

events.text: 'Ten thousand years!' the ministers shout, kneeling in rows round the altar, and the king sits on the golden chair at the top of it with the dawn coming up grey behind. Ten thousand years. Everyone in the square knows it will not be ten. The king knows it best.

choices.text: Rise behind the chair so the whole capital sees

effects.log: You rise behind the golden chair, enormous and gold, in the grey dawn. The ministers stop shouting. The foreign envoys at the edge of the square go white. For one morning, a small country stands on its own ground with a dragon behind it, and everyone sees.

choices.text: Stay under the altar, holding it

effects.log: You stay down, holding the altar, while the shouting goes on above. The king does not look for you. The king knows where you are.

events.text: The empire does not last. The envoys come back with soldiers and treaties, and the king, the emperor, the last of the house, sits on the golden chair in the throne hall the night before the end, alone, in yellow, and looks up at the ceiling, where you are painted with seven claws. You could stay behind the chair. Or not.

choices.text: Go down into the earth and wait for a better age

effects.log: You go down, and leave the throne hall to its painted dragons. It is not a betrayal. The house is ending; it would end with you or without you. You wait in the deep earth for the next thing that needs a centre, and you remember the king in yellow on the golden chair for a very long time.

choices.text: Bless the last emperor, and let the house end in peace

effects.log: You come up into the empty throne hall in the night and lie round the golden chair, and the last emperor puts a hand on your head, once, and does not weep. The house ends the next day with signatures, not fire. Nobody is killed in the palace. It is the best ending a small house could have had.

choices.text: Stand behind the golden chair, for ever

effects.log: You stay behind the chair. You go up into the coffered ceiling of the throne hall as two dragons with seven claws, gold on red, and when the house ends the next day and the last emperor walks out of the hall for the last time, you are still there, over an empty chair, and you are there still.

events.text: Far below the terrace, in a valley you have not thought of in centuries, a young farmer of a very old family is clearing the weeds behind a ruined farmhouse to build again, and has found a little clay rice jar with a rotten straw cap, buried to the neck. {npc} lifts the cap. The jar is empty. The ground under it is warm.

choices.text: Remember the jar

effects.log: You remember it all at once, the way a smell brings back a year: the cold rice going warm, the grandmother's bows, the tenth-month cakes not shared outside the gate. This is the jar. This farmer is that family, generation upon generation on, and has knelt, without knowing why, exactly where the grandmother knelt.

choices.text: Send a breath of warmth up into the jar

effects.log: The empty jar goes warm under {npc}'s hands. {npc} pulls them back, then puts them on it again, and sits back on {his} heels in the weeds for a long time, and then gets up and goes to find new rice.

events.text: {npc} has filled the old jar with new rice and woven a new straw cap for it, badly, from a picture in an almanac. {He} has rebuilt the farmhouse round it, small and crooked. Every evening {he} sits on the step by the jar, tired, and says to it that it is a long job and somebody has to do it.

choices.text: Warm the jar every evening when {he} sits there

effects.log: Every evening, when {npc} sits down, the jar is warm. {npc} stops talking to it about the long job and starts talking to it about everything else: the neighbours, the weather, a person in the next village {he} likes. You listen to all of it, from the top of the sky. It is the best news you get all century.

choices.text: Send the farm one good harvest, and watch

effects.log: One good harvest, exactly enough, dry and on time. {npc} bows to the jar in the tenth month, deep, the way a grandmother bows. The ground there is very warm. You feel it from the terrace, like a hand on your back.

events.text: The tenth month. {npc} kneels at the jar to change the rice, as the grandmother did generations upon generations ago, and lifts the crooked straw cap, and the old rice inside is warm and smells of new straw. From the top of the sky you feel it like a call home. You could go back. You could go home to one farmhouse and one jar, and be the luck of one family, for ever.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and bless the house from far off

effects.log: You stay at the top of the sky, where you are needed, and send the jar your warmth from there, every tenth month, for as long as the family keeps it. They keep it a very long time. It is enough. It is more than enough.

choices.text: Visit for one winter, then go back

effects.log: You go down for one winter and lie under the crooked farmhouse, the size of the whole valley and as quiet as a clod of clay, and {npc} sleeps better than {he} ever has, and does not know why. In spring you go back up. You are lighter than you have been since the crossroads.

choices.text: Go home to the jar

effects.log: You go home. You set down the four directions and the centre and every crown and season, and go down, all the way down, to one farmhouse and one jar of rice with a crooked straw cap, and lie under it, warm. {npc}'s rice never runs short. {npc}'s children are never ill. You are the luck of one family, for ever, which was the first thing you ever were.

events.text: You notice it one spring: the elders under the zelkova trees decide things without asking anyone. A ditch, a debt, a widow's field, settled by sunset in a hundred villages. You did not tell them how. You only gave them a little of your weight, long ago, and they kept it.
events.arc: The Kingdom That Needed No Dragon

choices.text: Watch one council all day, from under the zelkova

effects.log: You watch. They argue badly, then well. The youngest elder is wrong and is told so, kindly. The widow gets her field. You are not needed at any point. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen.

choices.text: Give them one more thing to carry

effects.log: You give them the granaries, too. They are frightened for a year and then very good at it. The weight on your back is smaller than it has ever been.

events.text: The market scales in every five-day market in the kingdom read true, and you are not keeping them true any more. The merchants do it themselves, out of habit, and pride, and the memory of the grandmothers' silence. You try, once, to make a scale lie, to see. The merchant notices at once and has it mended.
events.arc: The Kingdom That Needed No Dragon

choices.text: Laugh, under the market

effects.log: You laugh, under the market square, and the packed earth shivers, and the merchant looks down, frowning, and then goes back to weighing. You are not needed here either. You are delighted.

choices.text: Let go of the measures for good

effects.log: You let go of the measures, all of them. Nothing changes. The rice weighs what it weighs. You feel one more thing slide off your back, like a sack set down at the end of a long road.

events.text: The examinations are honest. The ministers argue and then decide. The heir, a quiet young person who listens more than speaks, sits through every council and asks the one question nobody wants asked. The kingdom is governing itself, and you lie under it, and it does not lean on you at all.
events.arc: The Kingdom That Needed No Dragon

choices.text: Go to the heir in a dream and say nothing

effects.log: You go to the heir in a dream as a warm field at harvest, and say nothing. The heir walks across the field and sits down in the middle of it and is content. In the morning the heir says to the ministers that the kingdom is in good hands, and means theirs.

choices.text: Give the heir the last of the weight

effects.log: You give the heir the last of it: the succession itself, the choosing of who comes after. The heir takes it gravely and carries it well. There is almost nothing left on your back now. You feel the strange lightness of a field after harvest.

events.text: You try leaving for a year. You go up to the terrace and lie at the edge of the sky, and do not look down, and at the end of the year you come back and look. Nothing has fallen. Nobody noticed you had gone. The harvests came in, the scales were true, the heir listened. The kingdom does not need a dragon.
events.arc: The Kingdom That Needed No Dragon

choices.text: Come back, and stay, because you love it

effects.log: You come back anyway, not because they need you but because you want to be there, under the fields, listening to the elders argue. That is a different thing from being needed. It weighs nothing at all.

choices.text: Go up to the terrace, where you are needed

effects.log: You go back up to the four and the middle of the sky, where things are still heavy and somebody has to hold them. Below, the kingdom goes on without you, gladly. You look down at it sometimes, the way an old farmer looks at a field a child has taken over.

choices.text: Go, and let nobody notice

effects.log: You go. You shared the weight piece by piece until there was nothing left to carry, and now you set down the last thing, which is yourself. A council of elders, a fair scale, an honest examination, an heir who listens. The kingdom rules itself. One spring nobody notices that you have gone, and that is the whole of your monument.

events.text: In a village far below, a shaman in five colours is holding the Five Directions rite. The drums start. The shaman takes up the blue fan and spins to the east, and calls its emperor down, and in the sky the east, the Azure Dragon's banner, stirs. You feel it from the middle, the way you feel a hand-over.

choices.text: Watch the rite from the middle of the sky

effects.log: You watch. The shaman spins east, and the east answers with a little rain on the village roofs. The shaman does not stop. You realise the rite will go all the way round, and end in the middle.

choices.text: Warm the yard under the shaman's feet

effects.log: The yard goes warm under the shaman's bare feet, and the shaman stumbles, once, and then spins harder, faster, because the shaman knows exactly what that means.

events.text: White fan, to the west; the Tiger's banner answers with a cold clear wind. Red fan, to the south; a warm gust from the Bird. The shaman is spinning faster than a human should, the five-colour sleeves a blur, and the whole village is on its knees.

choices.text: Hold the yard steady so the shaman does not fall

effects.log: You hold the yard still under the spinning feet. The shaman does not fall. The west and the south pass through the village one after another, wind and warmth, and the children laugh, and their mothers hush them, and laugh too.

choices.text: Listen to how the village calls each one

effects.log: They call the west with fear, and the south with love, and the east with hope. You listen to how they will call the centre. You are, you find, a little nervous.

events.text: Black fan and bell, to the north; the Tortoise's banner answers with a single slow snowflake that takes the whole length of a drum roll to fall. Then the shaman stops spinning, all at once, and turns, and takes up the yellow fan, and faces the middle of the yard.

choices.text: Hold your breath

effects.log: You hold your breath. So does the village. The shaman stands with the yellow fan raised, looking straight up, and the drums stop, and in the silence you can hear the bonfire and nothing else at all.

choices.text: Let the snowflake land, and warm it

effects.log: The north's snowflake lands in the middle of the yard and melts at once, because the ground there is warm. The shaman sees it, and smiles, and lifts the yellow fan.

events.text: The shaman calls the Yellow Emperor of the Centre down. Last of the five, the one the rite has been turning toward all night. And everything leans in: the east, the west, the south, the north, the village, the year, all of it, toward the middle of a farmyard where a shaman is holding up a yellow fan, facing you.

choices.text: Come down to the yard as warmth in the ground

effects.log: You come down as warmth, only warmth, up through the yard. The bonfire leans toward the middle. Every farmer in the village feels it through the soles of their feet, and the shaman, eyes shut, laughs like a child. The harvest that year is the best in a thousand years, in that village, and nowhere else, so nobody else will believe it.

choices.text: Come down as yourself, gold, for a breath

effects.log: For one breath you are in the sky over the yard, gold and enormous, the whole of you, and every face in the village is turned up. Then you are gone. Nobody in that village is ever afraid of yellow again.

events.text: The rite is over, and it is not over. The shaman sleeps in the yard, worn out. But the five directions are still leaning in toward the middle, and they are waiting, and you understand what for. Not for a dragon that holds the centre. For the centre itself. Every hand-over of the seasons could be your breath. Every harvest could be weighed on your scale.

choices.text: Not yet. Lie down at the edge of the sky again

effects.log: Not yet. You lie down at the edge of the sky, and the five directions settle back to their places, patient, the way fields settle at dusk. There will be other rites. They will turn toward you again.

choices.text: Go down and sit by the sleeping shaman until dawn

effects.log: You go down and lie round the sleeping shaman in the cold yard, warm, until dawn. The shaman wakes, and sees nothing, and feels the warmth going out of the ground, slowly, and says thank you to the yard, and goes home. You go back up. It was the right night to be small.

choices.text: Become the centre

effects.log: You let go of being a dragon that holds the centre, and are the centre. Every hand-over of the seasons is your breath now; every harvest is weighed on your scale. In every village where a shaman spins to the five directions, the rite ends last at the middle of the yard, facing you, and the ground there is always warm.

events.text: In the eighteen days before autumn, high on the terrace, you remember the clay. Not as a story: as a smell. Yellow clay at the centre of a house site, warm as bread, the size of a fist, and feet above pacing out a house, four steps, turn. You were never so small, or so certain of what you were for.

choices.text: Let the memory come all the way

effects.log: It comes all the way. The spade, the posts, the first rain soaking down toward you like news, the jar, the grandmother's bow. You were the luck of one house. You have been the centre of a kingdom since. You are not sure which was harder.

choices.text: Put it away, and go back to the council

effects.log: You put it away. There is a case from the west waiting, and a song from the south. But the smell of the clay stays with you all season, warm, under everything.

events.text: Heaven speaks to you in the way it does, in a change of weight. It is willing, it says, to send you back: to the clay under a house site, in the eighteen days before autumn, warm and the size of a fist, remembering everything. To begin again, and do it all differently, or all the same.

choices.text: Ask what you would do differently

effects.log: You think about it for years. You would set things down sooner. You would leave a failing house earlier. You would listen to the jar longer. You would do almost everything else the same. You are not sure that is reason enough to go back.

choices.text: Say: not yet

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. Heaven, which has a great deal of patience, waits. The offer stays, the way a house site waits for a post.

events.text: The eighteen days before autumn again, and the offer is still there. Somewhere far below, somebody is digging a house site in the dead days, in spite of the old people, and at the centre of it the yellow clay is waiting to be warm.

choices.text: Stay, and finish what you are

effects.log: You stay. You are the middle of the sky, and there are cases from the four still to hear. Far below, the spade goes into ordinary cold clay, and a house goes up, and is a perfectly ordinary house, which is what most houses should be.

choices.text: Send the digging family a good house, and stay

effects.log: You send a little warmth down to the house site, enough for luck, not enough for a dragon. The posts go in straight. The family is happy there for a hundred years. You stay where you are.

choices.text: Go back to the clay

effects.log: You go back. Heaven sends you down through every age you lived, all the way down, to the clay under a house site in the eighteen days before autumn, warm, and the size of a fist, and remembering everything. Above you, feet are pacing out a house. Four steps, turn. This time you know what you are for.

events.text: On the nights the four directions do not sit, another court uses the terrace: the Court of the Four Spirits. The Tortoise, which records. A seat for the one who comes, a bird, often empty. A seat for the one who asks, and tonight, walking up the cloud stair without bending it, the one who asks: a qilin, come to be read. You lie by the middle, a coil of gold, and the court looks at you.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Shut your eyes and listen with the patience of farmland

effects.log: You shut your eyes. You are not asleep, and the court knows it, and the qilin, who does not yet know, walks very carefully round you, as if round a sleeping field. Its record is read. When it is done you breathe out, long, like wind over ripe barley, and the court takes that for an answer.

choices.text: Open one eye and watch the qilin walk

effects.log: You open one eye. The qilin walks the terrace in a measured step, and the cloud does not bend under it, and the grass of the world below, you would swear, stands a little straighter wherever its shadow falls. You shut the eye again. You have seen what you needed.

events.text: The qilin's record is long and has no battles in it. Not one. A walk that bends no grass, a vow never to strike, a village it could not defend and a city it would not strike for. The Tortoise has written it all. The court turns to the middle. You have one question, and you have kept it a long time.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Ask: why should a beast that never fought sit among us?

effects.log: You open both eyes, which nobody on the terrace has seen you do in an age, and ask it. The qilin is silent a long time. Whatever it answers, you shut your eyes again and say, "Good," because it answered honestly, and because the ones who know already are the ones you have to replace.

choices.text: Say "Good," without opening your eyes

effects.log: "Good," you say, eyes shut. The qilin does not know what you are approving. Neither, exactly, do you. The Tortoise writes it down anyway, and underlines it.

events.text: After long years of sittings, you go to the qilin alone at the edge of the terrace one evening and lie down beside it on the cloud, the way a field lies beside a road. There is a seat it could have for good. There is a further shape for a qilin, too, past this one. You do not know what it costs.
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Offer it the seat for good, and the further shape, and let it choose

effects.log: "You could stay," you say, "in this seat, for good. Or you could go on. There is a further shape. Very few have taken it. I do not know what it costs." The qilin listens without bending the cloud. Whatever it chooses, you will be awake the whole time it is gone, pretending to sleep.

choices.text: Lie beside it another century, saying nothing

effects.log: Another century of nothing, beside a qilin at the edge of heaven. It is, you think afterwards, the most restful century either of you has ever had. The land below has a very good harvest, and nobody knows why.

events.text: A human grandmaster has climbed to the summit nearest the middle of the sky and drawn a sword: {npc}, who stands at the very top of the world below. {He} wants to duel the Dragon of the Between-Seasons, and the stake is one season's weather. "If I win," {he} says, "my province gets the spring it needs."

choices.text: Accept the duel

ok.log: It is a good duel, the best you have had in a century, on a summit in a wind, and you hold the ground. {npc} goes down on one knee in the snow, laughing. You give {his} province the spring anyway. "That was not the stake," {he} says. "I know," you say.

fail.log: {npc} wins, fairly, on a summit in a wind, with a cut you did not see coming. You give {his} province the spring it needs, and a little more, because a stake is a stake. {He} bows very low. You will remember that cut for a long time. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ask {him} what the province needs, and give it without a duel

effects.log: {npc} tells you: a wet spring and a late frost, for three counties of terraced barley. You give it. {He} stands on the summit with the sword still drawn, not sure whether {he} has won or lost. "You should have fought me," {he} says. "Next century," you say.

events.text: {npc}, an old abbot from a temple in the hills, has come down to the crypt under the capital's great temple to ask one thing: whether it is permitted to dig in the eighteen days before the season, because the monks need a new well and the old people say no. {He} has walked nine days to ask.

choices.text: Say: wait the eighteen days. The water will be sweeter

effects.log: {npc} waits. On the nineteenth morning the monks dig, and hit sweet water at an arm's depth, in a place nobody expected. {He} sends you a jar of it, nine days' walk, carried by a novice who does not know where it is going.

choices.text: Say: dig, and I will hold the ground still

effects.log: "Dig," you say. "I will hold still." The monks dig in the forbidden days, terrified, and nothing goes wrong at all. {npc} writes in the temple chronicle that the earth may be asked, and will sometimes say yes. It is the first time anyone has written that down.

events.text: An immortal envoy of the Jade court has come to audit the centre: {npc}, with an abacus, a ledger and three clerks. {He} has audited the east, the west, the south and the north. Now {he} stands in the middle of the terrace with the ledger open, looking for something to count.

choices.text: Give {him} nothing to audit

effects.log: You give {npc} nothing. No treasury, no record, no court. Only warmth, and the weight of the land, and an empty middle. {He} stands there a whole day with the brush raised. At the end {he} writes, carefully: Nothing to audit. Then {he} looks at the word a long time, and underlines it, and bows.

choices.text: Show {him} the land below, and let {him} count the harvests

effects.log: You show {npc} the land below: every field, every granary, every market scale. {He} starts counting. {He} is still counting a decade later, and has stopped writing, and is just looking. "It balances," {he} says at last, astonished. "All of it. How?" You do not answer. You pretend to sleep.

events.text: A sovereign of a high court of heaven has come with a retinue: {npc}, who wants to be the centre of everything. {He} has conquered seven heavens and sits in the middle of each of them, and none of them holds still. "How do you do it?" {he} asks. "Tell me, and I will give you a heaven of your own."

choices.text: Say: lie down and let them lean on you

effects.log: "Lie down," you say. "Let them lean on you. Do not hold them. Let them hold themselves, and lean." {npc} stares at you as if you had spoken in a foreign language. {He} goes away and tries it, and comes back three centuries later, much lighter, to say it worked in one of the seven, and that {he} has given the other six away.

choices.text: Say: you cannot be the centre by sitting in it

effects.log: "The centre is where the four agree," you say. "Not where you sit." {npc} is offended, then thoughtful, then angry, then gone. A thousand years later you hear that {he} has stopped conquering. You do not know whether it was you.

events.text: A royal tutor comes to the crypt under the throne hall with three name tablets: {npc}, who has taught all three of the king's children and cannot choose between them. "You choose," {he} begs. "You see everything. Choose the heir for me."

choices.text: Refuse: choosing is the tutor's weight

effects.log: "That is your weight," you say, "and I will not take it from you." {npc} weeps, then sits down on the crypt floor and thinks all night. In the morning {he} chooses, well. You feel the choosing go out of your hands and into {his}, where it belongs.

choices.text: Tell {him} what each child does when nobody is watching

effects.log: You tell {npc} three small things: the eldest feeds the palace cats, the middle one lies, the youngest listens at doors and remembers. {npc} chooses the youngest. You have not chosen, quite. It weighs a little anyway.

events.text: A child from a drought village has walked to the middle of the capital and lain down flat on the stones of the palace square with an ear to the ground, the way the old stories say, to ask the dragon for rain. {npc} does not look up when the guards come. {He} is listening.

choices.text: Answer {him} with a warm breath through the stones

effects.log: The stones under {npc}'s cheek go warm. {He} sits up, eyes wide, and walks home without a word. When {he} gets there, nine days later, it has been raining in the village for two days, softly, the kind that soaks in.

choices.text: Ask the east, at the next council, for the child's rain

effects.log: At the next council you bring the east a case of your own: one village, one child, one ear to the ground. The east, who has never forgotten a boy's field long ago, rains on that village first that spring. {npc} grows up to be the village's headman, and never digs in the eighteen days.

events.text: A general of a foreign army that once burned temples in this land has come, very old, to the ruin of the sixty-four stones: {npc}, who was a young officer then. {He} kneels at the centre stone and says that {he} has dreamed of the burning every night for sixty years, and asks to be forgiven, or punished, {he} does not mind which.

choices.text: Forgive {him}

effects.log: The centre stone goes warm under {npc}'s hands. {He} does not need words. {He} sleeps that night on the grass among the sixty-four stones, and does not dream of fire, and in the morning goes home to die in {his} own country, lighter.

choices.text: Tell {him} to rebuild one thing before {he} dies

effects.log: "Not the pagoda," you say. "Something small. A well, a bridge, a schoolroom." {npc} builds a schoolroom in the village by the ruin with the last of {his} money and teaches in it, badly, in a foreign accent, until {he} dies. The children love {him}.

events.text: A geomancer has come to the middle of the land with a compass that will not settle: {npc}, who has spent a lifetime looking for the true centre of the world and finds it moves. Every year, {he} says, it is a little somewhere else. {He} wants to know where it will be next year.

choices.text: Say: wherever the four agree

effects.log: "Wherever the four agree," you say. {npc} writes it down, and then throws away the compass, and spends the rest of {his} life walking from village to village, finding the places where quarrels have just been settled, and marking them on a map. It is the strangest map in the world, and the most accurate.

choices.text: Let the compass settle, once, on you

effects.log: For one breath you let the needle find you. It swings, and settles, and points straight down at the ground under {npc}'s feet. {npc} kneels, very slowly, and puts a palm flat on the earth, and feels it warm. {He} never tells anyone where it was.

events.text: Somewhere in the land, at one of ten thousand five-day markets, a rice merchant has hollowed the weights again. You feel it from the middle of the sky the way you feel a stone in a shoe: one scale, out of true, and a queue of grandmothers paying a tenth too much.

choices.text: Split the false weights in front of the market

effects.log: The hollow weights split on the scale with a crack like a twig, and the lead runs out of them into the dust. The grandmothers say nothing at all, which is worse than shouting. The merchant sells the rest of the rice at a fair price by noon.

choices.text: Make the scale read true, quietly

effects.log: The scale reads true, however the merchant leans. The merchant sweats, swaps weights, leans again. True. True. By the end of the day the merchant has given up and is honest, out of sheer exhaustion. It may last a year.

choices.text: Leave it to the market elders

effects.log: You leave it. The next market day the elders weigh the merchant's weights in front of everyone. They do not need you. You are very pleased, and a little hurt, and mostly pleased.

events.text: {npc}, the ruler of the house on your back, has come down into the crypt again, alone, with a lamp and a petition: a famine in one province, a rebellion in another, an ambassador who will not leave. {He} reads it to the floor and waits for the floor to answer.

choices.text: Answer one thing, and leave the rest to {him}

effects.log: You answer the famine: open the southern granaries, now. The rest you leave to {npc}. {He} goes back up the stair frowning, and deals with the rebellion and the ambassador alone, not very well, and then better.

choices.text: Answer everything

effects.log: You answer all of it, clearly, in order. {npc} goes back up and does exactly what you said, and everything goes well, and the next petition is longer. You feel it settle on your back with the others.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let {him} decide

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} waits until the lamp gutters, then sighs, and gets up, and decides alone. It is not the decision you would have made. It is not a bad one.

events.text: Two heirs of the house on your back are quarrelling over the succession again, in the courtyard, in front of the ministers, and the ministers are taking sides. You can feel the court splitting down the middle like a log.

choices.text: Crack the flagstone between them

effects.log: A flagstone cracks between the two heirs with a sound like a gong. Both of them stop. Both of them look down. The ministers go very quiet. The quarrel goes on, but indoors, and politely, and without daggers.

choices.text: Give the quarrel to the council of ministers

effects.log: You send the chief minister a dream: a scale with two weights on it, and nine hands steadying it. The council takes the quarrel off the heirs' hands, slowly and unwillingly, and settles it in a year. Nobody is happy. Nobody dies.

choices.text: Let them quarrel

effects.log: You let them. Some quarrels have to be had. It costs the house a summer of bad tempers and two ministers' careers. In the autumn the heirs are, to everyone's astonishment, friends.

events.text: A courtier has reported a yellow cloud over the palace at the New Year: the dragon blesses the king, the house will last ten thousand years. There was no cloud. The court chronicler is waiting, brush raised, to write it in the annals.

choices.text: Send a real cloud, grey, that rains on the courtier

effects.log: A small grey cloud forms over the palace in a clear sky and rains, only on the courtier. The chronicler writes that down instead. The court laughs for a month, and the next omen reported is a true one.

choices.text: Let the chronicler write it, and add a note

effects.log: The chronicler writes the omen, and then, in smaller characters underneath, adds: no one else saw it. You feel a great fondness for chroniclers.

choices.text: Do nothing; omens are humans' business

effects.log: You do nothing. The omen goes into the annals and nobody believes it. Most omens are like that. You have better things to hold up.

events.text: Out of council, on an ordinary evening, one of the four comes to the middle on its own: a banner leaning in from its side of the terrace, quiet, with no case to bring. It only wants to sit near the warm for a while. Tonight it is the west, frost on the white silk.

choices.text: Lie still and let it sit

effects.log: You lie still. It sits. Neither of you says anything. When it goes, the frost on its banner has melted a little at the edge nearest you, and it does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Ask about its day

effects.log: You ask. It is a little startled, and then tells you, at length, about an orchard in the west and a ghost that finally went home. You listen to all of it. Guardians are seldom asked about their days.

events.text: In the eighteen days before the season, the old season comes to the middle and asks, as they sometimes do, to stay a few days more. It has a reason. They always have a reason.

choices.text: Grant three days

effects.log: Three days. The old season spends them carefully, finishing something only it knows about, and hands the year over on the fourth morning with a bow. The farmers below notice nothing but a little late warmth.

choices.text: Refuse kindly, and take the year from it

effects.log: You take the year out of its arms gently, the way you would take a tired child, and hand it on. The old season goes away sulking and is grateful by the next hand-over.

choices.text: Pretend to sleep through the asking

effects.log: You pretend to sleep. The old season asks twice, hears itself, and hands the year over on time without another word.

events.text: Somewhere far below, an old farmer has left one field fallow this year, the way the old people say: one year in seven, let the ground rest. The farmer stands at its edge at dusk, looking at it, and says to it that it has earned a year off.

choices.text: Rest there with it for the winter

effects.log: You come down and rest under the fallow field for one winter, very small, very quiet. The weight comes out of you slowly, like frost out of ploughed ground. In spring the field is the best in the valley. So are you.

choices.text: Warm the field so the snow melts in the middle

effects.log: The snow melts in a ring in the middle of the field. The old farmer sees it the next morning and laughs, alone, and says aloud that the ground is pleased with the arrangement. It is.

events.text: Earth dams water: you have grown too heavy. This year the wells go dry one by one across the middle of the land, and the rice stands brown in cracked paddies, and the farmers stand at the dry wells looking down, at you.

choices.text: Open a spring with your own body

effects.log: You shift your weight off one valley, painfully, the way a sleeper rolls off a numb arm, and a spring breaks out of the hillside where you were. One valley drinks. The others wait. You understand that your own growing did this. (-5 health)

choices.text: Share the burden with the humans above

effects.log: You give the calamity to the humans to carry with you: granaries opened, roads cleared, elders sent from village to village. They carry it badly, then better. The wheel is still uneven. Hold the Between-Days, or turn it, before the next one.

choices.text: Lie still and feel where the wheel is uneven

effects.log: You lie still and feel it: one phase too strong, the one it overcomes too weak. The calamity is the wheel telling you so, the only way it can. You will have to even it.

events.text: Wood breaks earth: a spring too strong. The roots split the terraces this year, and in the summer rains the fields slide downhill in whole sheets, terraces and all, onto the roads below.

choices.text: Hold the terraces together with your back

effects.log: You put your back under the worst of the slopes and hold them while the rains come. Most stay up. Your back aches all summer with the roots of a thousand hills. (-5 health)

choices.text: Share the burden with the humans above

effects.log: You give the calamity to the humans to carry with you: granaries opened, roads cleared, elders sent from village to village. They carry it badly, then better. The wheel is still uneven. Hold the Between-Days, or turn it, before the next one.

effects.log: You lie still and feel it: one phase too strong, the one it overcomes too weak. The calamity is the wheel telling you so, the only way it can. You will have to even it.

events.text: Fire melts metal: a summer of fires. A county armoury burns this year with the plough-blades in it, and half the harvest with it, and the smiths stand in the ashes holding lumps of melted iron.

choices.text: Draw the heat down out of the forges

effects.log: You draw the heat down into yourself until the fires gutter. The smiths start again in the ashes. You are hot all through, like a hearthstone, for a decade. (-5 health)

effects.log: You give the calamity to the humans to carry with you: granaries opened, roads cleared, elders sent from village to village. They carry it badly, then better. The wheel is still uneven. Hold the Between-Days, or turn it, before the next one.

events.text: Metal cuts wood: the forges are never cold this year. The hills are stripped for charcoal, the armies go through the forests, and the bare slopes come down in the rain on the villages under them.

choices.text: Shake the roads so the armies turn back

effects.log: The ground shivers under the marching columns, and the horses refuse it, and the armies go home grumbling about bad omens. Some of the forests are saved. The hills will take a lifetime to grow back. (-5 health)

effects.log: You lie still and feel it: one phase too strong, the one it overcomes too weak. The calamity is the wheel telling you so, the only way it can. You will have to even it.

events.text: Water quenches fire: a cold, wet summer. The hearths will not stay lit this year, and the rain never stops, and the rice never ripens in the ear. The almanac-makers are burning their almanacs to keep warm.

choices.text: Warm the ground under the hearths

effects.log: You warm the ground under forty villages, a hearth at a time, until the floors are warm enough to sleep on. The rice still fails. Nobody freezes. (-5 health)

effects.log: You give the calamity to the humans to carry with you: granaries opened, roads cleared, elders sent from village to village. They carry it badly, then better. The wheel is still uneven. Hold the Between-Days, or turn it, before the next one.

events.text: The court astronomers are making the new almanac, and they have come to the eighteen days before autumn, and argued for a month. One faction wants to cut the days of earth out of the calendar as peasant superstition. One wants to keep them. A young astronomer has gone out into the night and lain down on the observatory floor.

choices.text: Let the young astronomer feel the days turn

effects.log: You let the young astronomer feel it through the floor: the year turning, slow and enormous, around a middle. The young astronomer gets up shaking and goes back in and argues for the eighteen days until dawn, and wins.

choices.text: Let them cut it, and see

effects.log: You let them cut the days of earth from the almanac. Nothing happens to the seasons; the seasons do not read almanacs. But the farmers, following the new calendar, dig in the dead days, and you feel every spade.

events.text: The new almanac has gone out to every county. In the eighteen days before autumn the farmers who follow it are digging new walls, moving graves, sinking wells. Some of the walls fall. Some of the wells come up bitter. The old people shake their heads and say nothing, very loudly.

choices.text: Hold the ground still under every spade

effects.log: You hold still under ten thousand spades. It is exhausting, like being tickled for eighteen days. Not one wall falls. The almanac-makers, hearing this, say the old days were superstition after all. You are too tired to mind. (-5 health)

choices.text: Let the bitter wells teach them

effects.log: You let the wells dug in the dead days come up bitter, and the walls raised in them lean. By the next year the farmers have quietly gone back to the old days, almanac or no almanac.

events.text: The young astronomer, now old and the chief of the observatory, has written a treatise on the eighteen days and why the year needs a middle to turn on. Nobody at court will read it. It lies on a shelf. On the last night of the eighteen days the old astronomer lies down on the observatory floor again, as once before.

choices.text: Warm the floor, once, in thanks

effects.log: The floor goes warm under the old astronomer's back, the way it did long ago. The old astronomer laughs and says, to the stars, "I knew it," and sleeps there till dawn, happier than any treatise could have made anyone.

choices.text: Let the treatise be found, later

effects.log: You let it lie. Two hundred years later a clerk dusting the shelf opens it and reads it in one night and copies it, and it goes into every almanac after. The old astronomer never knew. You did.

events.text: The newest almanac, from the press of the capital, has a little picture at the start of each season: a coil of yellow in the middle of a ring of four colours, and under it, in small characters, the eighteen days. Nobody at the observatory remembers who decided to put it there.

choices.text: Look at it a long time

effects.log: You look at the little picture a long time, from very far away. It is not a good likeness. It is the best thing anyone has ever made of you, because it is in every farmhouse in the land, hanging by the kitchen door.

choices.text: Send the printers a good harvest

effects.log: The printers' county has the best harvest in a generation. The printers do not connect it with anything. The almanac sells well. Everyone is happy, which is the purpose of an almanac.

events.text: A heavenly immortal has come to the edge of the terrace at dawn, from the east: {npc}, who was once a king of a house you upheld, and who stood on your head on the hill east of the capital, long ago, and was carried up. {He} has the same way of standing. {He} bows to you as an old friend bows.

choices.text: Ask how heaven has treated {him}

effects.log: "Kindly," says {npc}. "It is very quiet. Nobody asks me anything." {He} smiles. "I miss being asked things." You think about that. It is the most honest thing a king has ever said to you.

choices.text: Lie beside {him} at the edge and look east together

effects.log: You lie at the eastern edge together and look down at the hill where it happened, very small and green. Neither of you says anything for a whole morning. It is the best morning you have had in a century.

events.text: {npc} has been asked to testify at the council about the house you upheld: whether you were just to it, and to the kings after {him}. {He} stands at the edge of the circle in plain robes, and the four banners wait.

choices.text: Let {him} say whatever {he} likes

effects.log: {npc} says that you were heavy, sometimes, and silent when {he} wanted an answer, and that you carried {him} up from the hill when {he} was dead and frightened, and that {he} would be your king again tomorrow. The four banners bow. The clerk does not write anything; the clerk is crying.

choices.text: Ask {him} to say what you did wrong

effects.log: "You held on too long, once," says {npc}, "to my grandson, who was cruel." It is true. You have known it for a long time. Hearing it said aloud in front of the four takes something heavy off your back that you did not know was there.

events.text: {npc} comes to say goodbye: heaven is sending {him} down to be born again, as a farmer this time, {he} hopes, in a valley with a warm rice jar. {He} asks you to keep an eye on {him}.

choices.text: Promise to keep the jar warm

effects.log: "I will keep the jar warm," you say. {npc} laughs, and goes down the stair, and is born the next spring in a valley you know, to a family that changes the rice every tenth month. The jar is very warm that year.

choices.text: Say: you will not need me

effects.log: "You will not need me," you say. "You never did, much." {npc} looks at you a long moment, then bows the way a king bows, and goes down. You watch the valley for a hundred years anyway. The farmer is fine. Better than fine.

events.text: A human has come to the middle of the land, a human who stands almost at your level, which almost no human does: {npc}. {He} sits down on a bare hilltop with both palms flat on the earth, and says to the ground: "You carry too much. Give me some of it."

choices.text: Give {him} a little, to see

effects.log: You give {npc} the smallest thing you are carrying: the weather of one county for one year. {He} goes grey in the face, and holds it, and does not drop it. At the end of the year the county has had perfectly ordinary weather. {He} lies down on the hilltop and sleeps for a month.

choices.text: Ask {him} why

effects.log: "Because somebody stood in your place once, for a season, before you came," {npc} says, "and told me what it weighed. I have been getting strong enough ever since." {He} keeps both palms on the earth while you think about it.

events.text: {npc} has come back to the hilltop. {He} wants more. "A province," {he} says. "A season. A king's decision. Anything. I am ready." {His} hands, flat on the earth, are steady.

choices.text: Give {him} a season to hold

effects.log: You give {npc} the hand-over from winter to spring, in the eighteen days, for one year. {He} holds it. Spring comes in a day late and very gently. {npc} sits on the hilltop afterwards weeping with exhaustion and pride, and you feel lighter than you have in an age.

choices.text: Say: you have done enough. Go and live

effects.log: "Enough," you say. "Go and live. Someone at your level should have a life, too." {npc} argues, and then laughs, and goes down the hill. You hear later that {he} founded a school for village elders, and that it is very good.

events.text: {npc} is old now, even for a human at the top of the world. {He} comes to the hilltop one last time, with a younger human beside {him}, and puts the younger one's palms flat on the earth next to {his} own. "This one is next," {he} says. "When I am gone, give this one a little. Not too much."

choices.text: Promise, and warm both pairs of hands

effects.log: You warm the ground under both pairs of hands at once. The younger one gasps. {npc} smiles. You will give the younger one a little, when it is time. Not too much. You have learned how much is too much from {npc}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} learned from the weight

effects.log: "That it is lighter shared," says {npc}, "and that sharing it is heavier than carrying it alone, at first." {He} pats the earth. "You knew that." You did not, not until {him}.

events.text: An ordinary day at the centre. From here you can feel all of it at once: forty thousand fields, nine thousand markets, a crying child in the north, a wedding in the south, a magistrate making a bad decision in the west and an elder making a good one in the east. None of it needs you, exactly. All of it leans on you a little.

choices.text: Feel all of it, and hold none of it

effects.log: You feel it all and hold none of it. It leans on you the way a crowd leans on a wall, lightly, without noticing. The day goes by. Nobody below knows you were there. That is the best kind of day at the centre.

choices.text: Pick one small thing and help it

effects.log: The crying child in the north. You warm the floor under the child's sleeping mat until the crying stops. Forty thousand fields go on without you for an hour. Nothing falls. You knew it would not.

events.text: The four come to the middle together, out of council, for no reason. East, west, south, north. They do not bring cases. They sit at the edge of the gold, and the south hums, and the north writes nothing down for once, and you understand that they have come to rest, the way people come in from the fields to a warm floor.

choices.text: Let them rest on you

effects.log: They rest. It weighs nothing. It is the lightest thing you have ever carried: four tired guardians at the end of a long age, with nothing to ask.

choices.text: Shut your eyes and pretend to sleep, so they can

effects.log: You pretend to sleep, so that they will. One by one, they do. The terrace is quiet all night. In the morning the east rains a little by accident on the west, and the west does not mind.

events.text: An age at the centre, near enough. The grey clerk of the council, very old now, comes to ask whether you would like the minutes of your first century read back to you. The clerk has kept them all, including the ones the south set fire to.

choices.text: Listen to them all

effects.log: The clerk reads for a year. It is mostly you saying nothing, and "Good," and once a question. Listening to it, you find you are proud of how little you said. The clerk, at the end, says that the minutes have never been so short, or so useful.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to read only the burned parts

effects.log: The clerk reads the burned parts, which are mostly gaps. You fill them in from memory, and the clerk writes them down, and the south listens, embarrassed and delighted, to the record of every page it ever burned.
